title: Kashrut
subtitle: The holiness of the Jewish table
intro: Kashrut turns every meal into the fulfillment of a mitzvah. In this section you will learn where in the Torah the food laws come from, which animals, birds and fish are permitted, what shechitah is, how meat and milk are kept apart, how a kosher kitchen is set up, and how the different movements of Judaism approach kashrut.

overview.why: Kashrut makes ordinary food part of holiness: the Torah links the food laws with the words “sanctify yourselves and be holy,” and the Talmud likens a person’s table to the altar. The section shows where the prohibitions come from, how a kosher kitchen is set up, and why, at giyur, they are accepted as a mitzvah and not as a diet. In life, kashrut gathers a home and a community around a table at which any Jew can eat.
overview.examFocus: At the beit din you are almost always asked what kashrut means to you and how you live by it: what you do not eat, how you keep meat and milk apart, where you get meat, and what you will do when you are a guest. What is wanted is not a list of terms, but an honest answer in your own words and a clear understanding that kashrut is a chok, a commandment of the Almighty. In advance, talk through with your rabbi your custom of waiting, the hechsher you rely on, and how your kitchen is set up.
goals: After this section you will be able to explain that kashrut is a mitzvah of holiness, and not a diet
After this section you will be able to name the signs of kosher animals, fish and birds, with examples
After this section you will be able to describe the path of meat: shechitah, inspection, blood, chelev and the gid ha-nasheh
After this section you will be able to separate meat and milk and say how long to wait
After this section you will be able to explain dishes, a hechsher, and the differences in kashrut among the movements

deeper.title: The food laws in the Torah
deeper.text: Read Vayikra 11 and Devarim 14:3–21: there are the signs of animals and fish, the forbidden birds, and the words about holiness. This is the written basis of everything asked at the beit din about kashrut.

deeper.title: The table and the words of the Torah
deeper.text: In Pirkei Avot 3:3 (in some editions 3:4) there is the teaching about three who ate at one table and spoke words of Torah. This helps you see kashrut not only as a list of prohibitions, but also as service at an ordinary meal.

deeper.title: Practice in the Kitzur Shulchan Aruch
deeper.text: In the Russian “Kitzur Shulchan Aruch,” the salting of meat (chapter 36) and the laws of dishes (chapter 37) are set out briefly. Read it alongside the lessons on meat and the kitchen, and check the details of a particular case with your rabbi.

deeper.title: Kashrut as a way of life
deeper.text: In H. Donin’s book “To Be a Jew,” kashrut is shown as an everyday home: shopping, the kitchen and guests. That makes it easier to answer at the beit din in your own words about life, and not with a list of terms.

deeper.title: Kashrut in the Masorti movement
deeper.text: A survey of Conservative Judaism shows that kashrut there is binding halacha, but on wine, cheese and food prepared by a non-Jew the decisions are more lenient than the Orthodox ones. Check this with the rabbi of your community.

deeper.title: Kashrut as an informed choice
deeper.text: CCAR responsa and guides, and the practice of the Progressive communities of ROOPI, help you understand how Reform Judaism approaches kashrut: knowledge of the laws, the ethical side of food, and a personal but serious commitment, and not a turning away from the subject. Read this together with the lessons on the kitchen and on the movements.

lessons.title: What kashrut is, and why it is needed
keyIdeas: Kashrut comes from the word “kasher,” “fit”: the laws of what a Jew eats, how food is obtained and prepared, and what it is not mixed with.
The basis is Vayikra 11 and Devarim 14:3–21; the Oral Torah (Chullin, the Rambam, Yoreh De'ah) explains how these laws are to be fulfilled.
Kashrut is in large measure a chok: it is kept because the Almighty so commanded, and not out of disgust and not as a diet.
The Torah links food with holiness; the commentators also see the training of character, discipline, and the preservation of the people.
A table with blessings and words of Torah is likened to the altar; of the food laws, the descendants of Noach are given only ever min ha-chai.

blocks.text: The word “kasher”

The word **kashrut** (Heb. כַּשְׁרוּת) comes from the root כ-ש-ר, which means “fit, suitable, proper.” In the Tanakh this root appears, for example, in the Book of Esther (8:5): “if it please the king, and if the matter is *proper* before the king.” In halacha, “kasher” is what one calls everything fit for use according to the law: not only meat and bread can be kasher, but also a Torah scroll, a mezuzah, a shofar, a mikveh. As applied to food, kashrut is the whole set of laws about what a Jew may eat, how food must be obtained and prepared, and what it may not be mixed with.
“fit”: food or an object that meets the requirements of halacha. In Yiddish and in everyday Russian, people often say “kosher.”
literally “torn”: in the Torah, an animal torn by a beast, or one that has a fatal defect; in everyday speech this is the name for any food that is not kasher (“treif”).

blocks.he: וְאַנְשֵׁי קֹדֶשׁ תִּהְיוּן לִי וּבָשָׂר בַּשָּׂדֶה טְרֵפָה לֹא תֹאכֵלוּ
blocks.translit: Ve'anshei kodesh tihyun li uvasar basadeh treifa lo tokhelu
blocks.ru: And you shall be holy people to Me, and you shall not eat meat torn in the field

blocks.text: Where the Torah speaks of this

The main food laws are written in two chapters of the Torah: **Vayikra (Leviticus) 11** and **Devarim (Deuteronomy) 14:3–21**. There the signs of permitted animals and fish are listed, and the forbidden birds and insects. Other prohibitions are scattered through the whole Torah: the prohibition of blood (Vayikra 17:10–14; Devarim 12:16, 23), the prohibition of a certain fat — chelev (Vayikra 7:23–25), the prohibition of the sciatic nerve — the gid ha-nasheh (Bereshit (Genesis) 32:33), the prohibition of meat with milk (Shemot (Exodus) 23:19; 34:26; Devarim 14:21), the prohibition of an animal that died of itself — a neveilah (Devarim 14:21), and of what is torn — a treifa (Shemot 22:30).

The Written Torah gives the foundation, and the Oral Torah explains how to fulfill it: how to perform shechitah, by what signs to recognize kosher birds, how long to wait between meat and milk. These laws are set out in detail in the Talmudic tractate **Chullin**, codified by the Rambam in the “Mishneh Torah” (Laws of Forbidden Foods and Laws of Shechitah), and then in the **Shulchan Aruch**, in the section **Yoreh De'ah**. A short practical presentation is in the “Kitzur Shulchan Aruch,” which you can read in Russian.

items: which animals, birds, fish and insects are permitted as food;
how an animal must be slaughtered (shechitah) and inspected after slaughter;
the prohibition of blood, of forbidden fat (chelev) and of the sciatic nerve (gid ha-nasheh);
the prohibition of mixing meat with milk;
the requirements for dishes and the kitchen;
special laws about wine, bread and food prepared by non-Jews — these are mostly enactments of the sages.

differs.text: Reform Judaism does not regard the laws of kashrut as binding. Each Jew decides for themselves which of them to observe, but does so consciously, having studied the tradition. More on this is in lesson 6.

blocks.text: The laws of permitted food are commandments of the Torah, and they have not been “abolished” and have not been replaced by a new teaching about food. Like the other mitzvot, kashrut belongs to the eternal covenant: “do not add and do not take away” (Devarim 13:1). A person may not yet keep everything, but the rule of the Torah itself does not cease to be the rule.
A chok — a law without an explanation

The sages divide the commandments into several groups. **Mishpatim** are laws clear to the mind: the prohibition of theft, murder, deceit. **Edot** (“testimonies”) are commandments that recall events of history, for example the festivals. **Chukim** are decrees whose meaning the Torah does not reveal. Classic examples of chukim are the law of the red heifer (Bamidbar 19), the prohibition of shaatnez (a mixture of wool and linen), and, in large measure, the laws of kashrut. The Torah does not say why the pig is forbidden and the cow permitted; it only names the signs.
a decree-commandment, fulfilled because the Almighty so commanded, even if the reason is unknown.
Let a person not say: “Pork is repulsive to me.” Let him say: “I would want it, but what can I do if my Father in Heaven has forbidden it to me.”
blocks.ref: Sifra; cited by Rashi on Vayikra 20:26

blocks.text: This idea matters for a candidate for giyur. Kashrut is not a diet and not a matter of taste. A Jew refrains from certain foods not because they are unpleasant to him, but because he has taken the commandments upon himself. That is why, at the beit din, people often ask not only “what is forbidden,” but also “why do you keep this.”
And yet, why? The commentators' explanations
Although kashrut is a chok, Jewish thinkers have looked for meaning in it. These explanations are not a condition for keeping it; they are an attempt to understand what the laws teach:

items: **Holiness.** The Torah itself links the food laws to holiness: “sanctify yourselves and be holy, for I am holy” (Vayikra 11:44); “for you are a holy people to the L-rd your G-d… do not eat any abomination” (Devarim 14:2–3).
**Shaping character.** The Ramban (on Vayikra 11:13) explains that the forbidden birds are birds of prey, and their nature can pass to the one who eats them, fostering cruelty.

**Health.** The Rambam wrote in the “Guide for the Perplexed” (3:48) that forbidden food is harmful to the body. But many authors, such as Abarbanel, objected: if it were only a matter of hygiene, the Torah would be a medical book.
**Self-discipline.** Every meal becomes a choice: a person learns to say “no” to desire, and this skill carries over into the whole of life.
**People and family.** For centuries kashrut set Jews apart from the surrounding cultures and preserved the community. A kosher home is open to every Jew: anyone can eat there.

blocks.he: וְהִתְקַדִּשְׁתֶּם וִהְיִיתֶם קְדֹשִׁים כִּי קָדוֹשׁ אָנִי
blocks.translit: Vehitkadishtem viheyitem kedoshim ki kadosh ani
blocks.ru: Sanctify yourselves and be holy, for I am holy

blocks.text: The table as an altar

The Talmud says: while the Temple stood, the altar atoned for Israel, and now “a person's table atones for him” (Berachot 55a). Kashrut, together with the blessings before and after eating, washing the hands before bread, and words of Torah at the meal, turns an ordinary dinner into divine service. That is why it is customary to put salt on the bread, as on the offerings in the Temple (Vayikra 2:13).

blocks.ru: A person's table atones for him

blocks.text: Three who ate at one table and spoke words of Torah there are as if they had eaten from the table of the Almighty.
Kashrut and non-Jews

The descendants of Noach, that is, all of humanity, were given only one of the food laws: the prohibition of eating a part cut from a living animal, **ever min ha-chai** (Bereshit 9:4). All the other laws of kashrut are mitzvot given to Israel. In accepting giyur, a person takes them upon themselves: before giyur, kashrut is preparation and study; after giyur, it is an obligation.

Start gradually, preferably together with a mentor. The usual path: first stop eating forbidden animals and seafood, then stop mixing meat and dairy, then switch to products with a hechsher, and finally kasher the kitchen.

cards.front: What does the word “kasher” mean?
cards.back: “Fit, suitable” (root כ-ש-ר). The word is used for food, and also for a Torah scroll, a mezuzah or a shofar that is fit according to halacha.

cards.front: In which chapters of the Torah are the main laws about permitted animals?
cards.back: Vayikra (Leviticus) 11 and Devarim (Deuteronomy) 14:3–21.

cards.front: What does “treifah” literally mean?
cards.back: “Torn”: an animal torn by a beast (Shemot 22:30). In everyday use, any non-kosher food.

cards.front: What is a chok?
cards.back: A decree-mitzvah whose reason the Torah does not explain. Kashrut is the classic example.

cards.front: How do mishpatim differ from chukim?
cards.back: Mishpatim are understandable to reason (the prohibition of theft); chukim are kept as a decree of the Almighty (kashrut, shatnez, the red heifer).

cards.front: Which verse links kashrut to holiness?
cards.back: “Sanctify yourselves and be holy, for I am holy” (Vayikra 11:44).

cards.front: According to the Sifra (cited by Rashi on Vayikra 20:26), what should one say about pork?
cards.back: Not “it disgusts me,” but “I would like to, but what can I do: my Father in Heaven has forbidden it.”

cards.front: How does the Ramban explain the prohibition of birds of prey?
cards.back: Their predatory nature can pass to a person and foster cruelty (Ramban on Vayikra 11:13).

cards.front: What reason for kashrut does the Rambam give in the “Guide for the Perplexed” 3:48?
cards.back: Benefit to health: forbidden food is harmful to the body. Other authors (Abarbanel) disputed this.

cards.front: Which food prohibition was given to all the descendants of Noach?
cards.back: Ever min ha-chai: the prohibition of eating a part of a living animal (Bereshit 9:4).

cards.front: What does “a person's table atones for him” mean?
cards.back: Since the destruction of the Temple, a table with kashrut, blessings and words of Torah is like the altar (Berachot 55a).

cards.front: In which section of the Shulchan Aruch are the laws of kashrut collected?
cards.back: Yoreh De'ah.

cards.front: Which tractate of the Talmud is devoted to shechitah and meat foods?
cards.back: Chullin.

cards.front: Into which three categories is food divided in a kosher kitchen?
cards.back: Meat (basari), dairy (chalavi) and neutral (parve).

cards.front: Why is salt put on the bread at a meal?
cards.back: In memory of the offerings in the Temple, which were salted (Vayikra 2:13): the table is like the altar.

cards.front: How does Reform Judaism approach kashrut?
cards.back: As a tradition that each person chooses consciously; the laws of kashrut are not considered binding.

cards.front: What are edot among the mitzvot?
cards.back: “Testimonies”: mitzvot that recall events of history, for example the festivals.

cards.front: Where in the Tanakh does the root כ-ש-ר appear in the sense of “right, pleasing”?
cards.back: In the book of Esther (8:5): “if it please the king, and the thing seem right before the king.”

cards.front: What does Pirkei Avot say about three who ate at one table?
cards.back: If they spoke words of Torah, it is as if they ate from the table of the Almighty (Avot 3:3, in some editions 3:4).

cards.front: What was Abarbanel's objection to explaining kashrut by hygiene?
cards.back: If it were only a matter of health, the Torah would be a medical book.

cards.front: What is the usual gradual path to kashrut?
cards.back: Give up forbidden animals and seafood → stop mixing meat and dairy → products with a hechsher → kasher the kitchen.

cards.front: Where does the Torah forbid what is torn (treifah) and carrion (neveilah)?
cards.back: Treifah: Shemot 22:30; neveilah: Devarim 14:21.

cards.front: What does kashrut mean before giyur and after it?
cards.back: Before giyur it is preparation and study; after giyur it is an obligation, since the laws of kashrut were given to Israel.

cards.front: Have the laws of kashrut been abolished by a “new teaching” about food?
cards.back: No. They are mitzvot of the Torah in an eternal covenant; “do not add to it and do not take away from it” (Devarim 13:1).

lessons.title: Permitted animals, birds and fish
keyIdeas: A mammal is kosher only if it has both signs at once: fully split hooves and chewing the cud (ma'alat gerah).
The camel, the shafan and the hare chew the cud but lack split hooves; the pig has split hooves but does not chew the cud.
A fish is kosher if it has fins and removable scales; it is parve and needs no shechitah; seafood is forbidden.
Birds are eaten only with a mesorah: chicken, turkey, duck, goose, pigeon, quail; the eggs of kosher birds are parve.
Insects are forbidden, except for four kinds of locust in communities with a tradition; honey is permitted, since the bee only collects it.

blocks.text: Four-legged animals: two signs

For mammals the Torah gives two signs, and they must be present **both at the same time**: the animal must have fully split hooves and chew the cud, that is, bring up swallowed food and chew it again. These rules apply both to domestic animals (behemah) and to wild animals (chayah).

blocks.he: כֹּל מַפְרֶסֶת פַּרְסָה וְשֹׁסַעַת שֶׁסַע פְּרָסֹת מַעֲלַת גֵּרָה בַּבְּהֵמָה אֹתָהּ תֹּאכֵלוּ
blocks.translit: Kol mafreset parsah veshosa'at shesa perasot ma'alat gerah babehemah otah tochelu
blocks.ru: Every animal that has split hooves, with a deep cleft in the hooves, and that brings up the cud, that you may eat

blocks.text: The Torah specifically names four animals that have only one sign and are therefore forbidden (Vayikra 11:4–7). The camel, the shafan (usually identified with the hyrax) and the hare outwardly “chew,” but do not have split hooves. The pig, on the contrary, has split hooves but does not chew the cud. That is why in Jewish culture the pig became the symbol of what is treif: it looks “kosher” on the outside, but it is not.

The book of Devarim (14:4–5) lists the permitted animals: among domestic animals, the ox, the sheep and the goat, and also seven kinds of wild animals, traditionally translated as deer, gazelle, roe deer, ibex and others; the exact identification of some names is disputed. In practice, kosher meat means beef, veal, lamb, goat, and sometimes venison. Pork, rabbit, horse meat, camel meat and the meat of all predators are forbidden.
“bringing up the cud”: one of the two signs of a kosher mammal.

A general rule applies: “what comes from the impure is impure” (Mishnah Bechorot 1:2). The milk of a camel or a mare, the eggs of non-kosher birds and the roe of non-kosher fish are forbidden. A well-known exception is **honey**: the bee is forbidden as food, but honey is not produced by its body; it is only collected and stored in it, so it is permitted (Bechorot 7b).
Fish: fins and scales

blocks.he: כֹּל אֲשֶׁר לוֹ סְנַפִּיר וְקַשְׂקֶשֶׂת בַּמַּיִם בַּיַּמִּים וּבַנְּחָלִים אֹתָם תֹּאכֵלוּ
blocks.translit: Kol asher lo snapir vekaskeset bamayim bayamim uvanechalim otam tochelu
blocks.ru: Everything in the water, in the seas and in the rivers, that has fins and scales, those you may eat

blocks.text: The Mishnah (Niddah 6:9) notes: every fish that has scales also has fins, but not the other way round. So in practice it is above all the scales that are checked. According to halacha these must be scales that can be removed without damaging the skin, as on a carp or a perch (Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De'ah 83). Fish needs no shechitah or salting to remove blood, and it is considered **parve**, neither meat nor dairy.

items: Kosher fish (examples): salmon, trout, carp, herring, cod, hake, pollock, tuna, mackerel, pike, zander, perch, tilapia.
Non-kosher: catfish, eel, shark, and also, according to the Orthodox position, sturgeon and beluga.
All “seafood” is forbidden: shrimp, crabs, crayfish, lobsters, mussels, oysters, squid, octopus; marine mammals are forbidden as well.
Caviar: red caviar from salmon is kosher (with supervision of production); black caviar from sturgeon is not.

blocks.text: A skinless fillet cannot be checked for scales. That is why fish is bought either whole, or with the skin on, or under kashrut supervision.
Birds: tradition matters more than signs

For birds the Torah gives no signs; instead it lists the forbidden species (Vayikra 11:13–19; Devarim 14:11–20); the Talmud counts 24 impure species (Chullin 63b). Among them are the eagle, the hawk, the owl, the raven, the stork and the ostrich. The Mishnah (Chullin 3:6) names the signs of a kosher bird: it is not a bird of prey, it has an “extra” (hind) toe and a crop, and the inner lining of its gizzard peels off easily by hand.

However, the names of the birds in the Torah cannot always be reliably identified. Therefore halacha ruled that only birds for which there is a **mesorah** are eaten: an unbroken tradition that our ancestors ate them (Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De'ah 82:2, Rema). The accepted kosher birds are chicken, turkey, duck, goose, pigeon and quail; some communities also have a tradition for pheasant or guinea fowl. The eggs of kosher birds are permitted and are parve.
“transmission, tradition”: here, the tradition confirming that a given bird is kosher.
When breaking eggs, it is customary to check each one for a blood spot; an egg with blood is not used (Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De'ah 66). That is why eggs are broken one at a time into a clear glass.
Insects

The Torah forbids all “swarming” creatures: insects, worms, reptiles, rodents (Vayikra 11:20–23, 41–44). The exception is four kinds of locust (Vayikra 11:22), but only the Yemenite and some North African communities have preserved the tradition of identifying them; other Jews do not eat locusts. The prohibition of insects is very strict: the Talmud (Makkot 16b) explains that by eating one small insect a person can transgress several Torah prohibitions at once.

That is why in a kosher kitchen vegetables, fruit and grains are checked. Particular care is taken with leafy greens (lettuce, cabbage, parsley, dill, cilantro), broccoli and cauliflower, strawberries, raspberries, blackberries, artichokes, and also flour (it is sifted), grains, legumes and dried fruit. A common method: soak the greens in water with a few drops of dish soap, rinse under a strong stream and examine the leaves against the light. There are products grown under supervision as “insect-free,” and lists issued by rabbinates (Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De'ah 84).
What is visible to the naked eye is forbidden. Microscopic organisms that can be seen only under magnification are not forbidden.
The food coloring carmine (E120) is made from cochineal insects, so products containing it are not kosher. This is one of the reasons why ready-made products are bought with a hechsher.

cards.front: What are the two signs of a kosher mammal?
cards.back: Fully split hooves and chewing the cud (ma'alat gerah), both signs at once (Vayikra 11:3).

cards.front: Which four animals does the Torah name as having only one sign?
cards.back: The camel, the shafan (hyrax) and the hare chew the cud but lack split hooves; the pig has split hooves but does not chew the cud (Vayikra 11:4–7).

cards.front: Which domestic animals does the Torah explicitly name as kosher?
cards.back: The ox, the sheep and the goat (Devarim 14:4).

cards.front: What are the signs of a kosher fish?
cards.back: Fins and scales (Vayikra 11:9); the scales must come off without damaging the skin.

cards.front: Why, in practice, is it the scales of a fish that are checked?
cards.back: Every fish with scales also has fins, but not the other way round (Mishnah Niddah 6:9).

cards.front: Are shrimp, squid and mussels kosher?
cards.back: No: all seafood without fins and scales is forbidden.

cards.front: Is black sturgeon caviar kosher?
cards.back: According to the Orthodox position, no: the sturgeon is not considered a kosher fish. Red salmon caviar is kosher with supervision.

cards.front: Which category does fish belong to?
cards.back: Parve: it is neither meat nor dairy, and needs no shechitah or salting.

cards.front: What is a mesorah with regard to birds?
cards.back: A tradition that our ancestors ate a given bird; only birds with a mesorah are eaten.

cards.front: Name the birds that are commonly considered kosher.
cards.back: Chicken, turkey, duck, goose, pigeon, quail.

cards.front: Which signs of a kosher bird does Mishnah Chullin 3:6 name?
cards.back: Not a bird of prey; a hind toe; a crop; a gizzard lining that peels off by hand.

cards.front: Why is honey kosher, even though the bee is forbidden?
cards.back: Honey is not produced by the bee's body; the bee only collects it (Bechorot 7b).

cards.front: What does “what comes from the impure is impure” mean?
cards.back: Products of non-kosher animals (mare's milk, raven's eggs, catfish roe) are forbidden (Mishnah Bechorot 1:2).

cards.front: Which insects does the Torah permit?
cards.back: Four kinds of locust (Vayikra 11:22); the tradition has been preserved mainly by Yemenite Jews.

cards.front: Which foods are checked for insects with particular care?
cards.back: Leafy greens, broccoli, cauliflower, strawberries, raspberries, flour, grains, dried fruit.

cards.front: Why are eggs broken one at a time into a glass?
cards.back: To check for a blood spot; an egg with blood is not used (Yoreh De'ah 66).

cards.front: How many impure species of birds does the Talmud count?
cards.back: 24 species (Chullin 63b); among them the eagle, hawk, owl, raven, stork and ostrich.

cards.front: Why is the prohibition of insects considered very strict?
cards.back: By eating one small insect, a person can transgress several Torah prohibitions at once (Makkot 16b).

cards.front: Are microorganisms visible only under magnification forbidden?
cards.back: No: what is visible to the naked eye is forbidden.

cards.front: Why are products with the coloring E120 not kosher?
cards.back: Carmine (E120) is made from cochineal insects.

cards.front: Why is fish bought whole, with the skin on, or under supervision?
cards.back: A skinless fillet cannot be checked for scales.

cards.front: What do the words “behemah” and “chayah” mean?
cards.back: Behemah means domestic animals, chayah means wild animals; the signs of kashrut are the same for both.

cards.front: Is horse meat forbidden?
cards.back: Yes. The lesson places horse meat among the forbidden meats, together with pork, rabbit and camel meat.

lessons.title: Shechitah, blood, chelev and gid ha-nasheh
keyIdeas: Without shechitah even a cow or a chicken is forbidden: one that died on its own or was killed another way is neveilah. Fish and locusts need no shechitah.
The Torah does not describe the method of slaughter, but it says “as I have commanded you”: the laws were handed down orally. The shochet cuts with a smooth chalaf.
After shechitah the organs are checked: a defect with which the animal would not have lived a year makes it treifah; in cattle the lungs are examined.
Blood is forbidden, “for the blood is the life.” Chelev is forbidden in the ox, sheep and goat; gid ha-nasheh is a sinew, forbidden in memory of Yaakov.
The remaining blood is removed by salting or broiling, and the liver only over fire. Meat is bought with a hechsher: a kosher species is not enough.

blocks.text: Why shechitah is needed

Even an animal of a kosher species, such as a cow, a sheep or a chicken, is forbidden as food if it was not slaughtered in a special way called **shechitah**. An animal that died on its own or was killed another way (by shooting, a blow, or stunning followed by death) is called **neveilah**, “carrion,” and the Torah forbids eating it (Devarim 14:21). Fish and locusts need no shechitah.

blocks.he: וְזָבַחְתָּ מִבְּקָרְךָ וּמִצֹּאנְךָ אֲשֶׁר נָתַן ה׳ לְךָ כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוִּיתִךָ
blocks.translit: Vezavachta mibekarcha umitzoncha asher natan Adonai lecha ka'asher tziviticha
blocks.ru: And you shall slaughter of your cattle and of your flock, which the L-rd has given you, as I have commanded you

blocks.text: The Written Torah does not describe the method of slaughter, but it says: “as I have commanded you.” From these words the Talmud (Chullin 28a) derives that the laws of shechitah were given to Moshe orally. This is a good example of how the Written Torah is inseparable from the Oral Torah.

Shechitah is a swift, continuous cut across the throat with a very sharp knife whose blade is perfectly smooth, without a single nick. The trachea and the esophagus are severed (in cattle, the greater part of both; in a bird, the greater part of one is enough), and with them the carotid arteries and jugular veins. Blood pressure in the brain drops sharply, the animal quickly loses consciousness, and most of the blood drains from the body. Jewish tradition sees in this an expression of the mitzvah of **tza'ar ba'alei chayim**, the prohibition of causing animals unnecessary suffering.

differs.text: Reform Judaism does not consider shechitah obligatory. Some Reform Jews still buy kosher meat out of respect for tradition and for the unity of the community; others choose vegetarianism or meat with an ethical label.

blocks.text: ritual slaughterer: a G-d-fearing Jew who has studied the laws of shechitah and received authorization (kabbalah) from a rabbi.
the knife for shechitah: long, very sharp, with an absolutely smooth blade; it is checked before and after every slaughter.

blocks.he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם אֲשֶׁר קִדְּשָׁנוּ בְּמִצְוֹתָיו וְצִוָּנוּ עַל הַשְּׁחִיטָה
blocks.translit: Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu melech ha'olam, asher kideshanu bemitzvotav vetzivanu al hashechitah
blocks.ru: Blessed are You, L-rd our G-d, King of the universe, who has sanctified us with His mitzvot and commanded us concerning shechitah
blocks.ref: The shochet's blessing (Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De'ah 19:1)

items: **Shehiyah**: pausing; the cut must be continuous.
**Derasah**: pressing; the knife moves back and forth and does not press down from above.
**Chaladah**: “concealment”; the blade must be visible the whole time and may not be hidden under the skin or the wool.
**Hagramah**: deviation; a cut outside the proper place on the neck.
**Ikur**: tearing; the trachea or esophagus is torn out rather than cut.

blocks.text: These are the five actions that invalidate shechitah (Chullin 9a; Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De'ah 23–24). If any one of them occurs, the animal is considered neveilah. After slaughtering a wild animal or a bird, the blood is covered with earth or ash, with a blessing: this is the mitzvah of **kisui ha-dam** (Vayikra 17:13).
Inspection: treifot and “glatt”

After shechitah the internal organs are examined. If the animal is found to have a defect because of which it would not have lived even a year (for example, a perforated organ or a damaged lung), it is **treifah** and forbidden, even if the shechitah was correct. The main kinds of such defects are listed in the Mishnah (Chullin 3:1). In cattle the lungs must be checked for adhesions, **sirchot**.

The word **glatt** (Yiddish for “smooth,” Hebrew *chalak*) means that the animal's lungs are completely smooth, without adhesions. Sephardim, following the Beit Yosef (Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De'ah 39), eat only such meat. Ashkenazim, following the Rema, allow certain easily removed adhesions, but today many of them also buy “glatt.” Strictly speaking, the term applies only to the lungs of cattle; a “glatt kosher” label on chicken or cheese is just a marketing way of saying “strict kashrut.”
The prohibition of blood

blocks.he: רַק חֲזַק לְבִלְתִּי אֲכֹל הַדָּם כִּי הַדָּם הוּא הַנָּפֶשׁ
blocks.translit: Rak chazak levilti achol hadam ki hadam hu hanefesh
blocks.ru: Only be firm not to eat blood, for blood is the soul

blocks.text: The prohibition of blood is repeated in the Torah many times (Bereshit 9:4; Vayikra 3:17; 7:26–27; 17:10–14; Devarim 12:16, 23–25), and for its deliberate violation the Torah assigns **karet** — "cutting off of the soul" (Vayikra 7:27). The explanation is given in the verse itself: blood is the bearer of life. A person is permitted to eat meat, but not the life of the animal. The prohibition concerns the blood of mammals and birds; the Torah does not forbid the blood of fish.
Chelev and gid ha-nashe

blocks.he: כָּל חֵלֶב שׁוֹר וְכֶשֶׂב וָעֵז לֹא תֹאכֵלוּ
blocks.translit: Kol chelev shor ve-chesev va-ez lo tochelu
blocks.ru: You shall eat no fat of ox, sheep, or goat

blocks.text: **Chelev** is certain kinds of fat around the stomach, kidneys, and intestines, which in the Temple was burned on the altar. Ordinary fat interspersed through the meat (*shuman*) is permitted. The prohibition of chelev applies only to domestic animals — the ox, sheep, and goat; the chelev of wild animals and of birds is permitted.

blocks.he: עַל כֵּן לֹא יֹאכְלוּ בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶת גִּיד הַנָּשֶׁה
blocks.translit: Al ken lo yochlu bnei Yisrael et gid ha-nashe
blocks.ru: Therefore the children of Israel do not eat the sciatic nerve

blocks.text: **Gid ha-nashe** is the sciatic nerve of the hind leg. The prohibition recalls the struggle of the patriarch Yaakov with the angel, who injured his hip. It applies to both domestic and wild animals, but not to birds. The removal of the chelev and the nerve is called **nikkur** (in Yiddish, "treibering") and requires a specialist. Outside Israel, because of the difficulty of this work, the hindquarters of the carcass (from which, for example, tenderloin and rump steak are taken) are usually sold to non-Jewish buyers; in Israel they are processed by specialist menakkrim.
Koshering meat with salt

The blood remaining in the meat after shechitah is removed by **salting** (melichah) or by roasting over an open fire. The order of salting is set out in the Kitzur Shulchan Aruch (ch. 36) and the Shulchan Aruch (Yoreh Deah 69):

items: Soak the meat in water so that it is covered, for about half an hour.
Let the water drain off.
Sprinkle it on all sides with salt of medium coarseness — not fine, so that it does not dissolve, and not too coarse, so that it does not roll off.
Leave it for an hour on a rack or a slanted board so that the blood drains off.
Shake off the salt and rinse the meat thoroughly, by custom three times.

blocks.text: The liver contains so much blood that it is koshered only by roasting over fire (Yoreh Deah 73). Meat that was not salted and rinsed within 72 hours of shechitah can be koshered only by roasting over fire. Ground meat is made from already koshered meat. Today almost all meat with a hechsher is sold already koshered, as stated on the packaging.

Practical conclusion: buy meat and poultry only at a kosher store or with a reliable hechsher. An animal of a kosher species, without shechitah, inspection, and removal of blood, is not yet kosher meat.

cards.front: What is shechitah?
cards.back: Ritual slaughter: a swift, continuous cut across the throat with a smooth, sharp knife, cutting through the trachea and the esophagus.

cards.front: From which verse is it derived that the laws of shechitah were transmitted orally?
cards.back: "And slaughter… as I have commanded you" (Devarim 12:21; Chullin 28a).

cards.front: What is nevelah?
cards.back: An animal that died on its own or was killed not by shechitah; eating it is forbidden (Devarim 14:21).

cards.front: Who is a shochet?
cards.back: A slaughterer: a G-d-fearing Jew who knows the laws of shechitah and has received a rabbi's authorization.

cards.front: What is the knife for shechitah called, and what must it be like?
cards.back: A chalaf: very sharp, with an absolutely smooth blade free of nicks.

cards.front: Which animals do not require shechitah?
cards.back: Fish and (kosher) locusts.

cards.front: Name the five violations that render shechitah invalid.
cards.back: Shehiyah (pausing), derasah (pressing), chaladah (hiding the knife), hagremah (deviating), ikkur (tearing).

cards.front: What is a treifah after a proper shechitah?
cards.back: An animal with a defect of the organs because of which it would not live out the year (Mishnah Chullin 3:1).

cards.front: What does "glatt" mean?
cards.back: "Smooth": the animal's lungs without adhesions (sirchot). Sephardim eat only such meat.

cards.front: Why does the Torah forbid blood?
cards.back: "For blood is the soul" (Devarim 12:23): a person may eat meat, but not the life of the animal.

cards.front: What punishment does the Torah assign for deliberately consuming blood?
cards.back: Karet — "cutting off of the soul" (Vayikra 7:27).

cards.front: What is chelev, and to whom does the prohibition apply?
cards.back: A special fat around the stomach, kidneys, and intestines; forbidden only in the ox, sheep, and goat (Vayikra 7:23).

cards.front: What is gid ha-nashe, and why is it forbidden?
cards.back: The sciatic nerve — in memory of Yaakov's struggle with the angel (Bereshit 32:33).

cards.front: What is the removal of the chelev and the sciatic nerve called?
cards.back: Nikkur (in Yiddish — "treibering").

cards.front: What is the order of salting meat?
cards.back: Soak for ~30 minutes, drain, salt on all sides, leave for an hour, rinse thoroughly (KSA 36).

cards.front: How is the liver koshered?
cards.back: Only by roasting over an open fire — it contains too much blood (Yoreh Deah 73).

cards.front: What is kisuy ha-dam?
cards.back: The commandment to cover with earth the blood of a wild animal or bird after shechitah (Vayikra 17:13).

cards.front: What part of the trachea and esophagus is cut in shechitah?
cards.back: For cattle — the greater part of both; for birds, the greater part of one is sufficient.

cards.front: Which commandment does tradition see in the swift cut of shechitah?
cards.back: Tzaar baalei chaim — the prohibition against causing animals unnecessary suffering.

cards.front: What blessing does the shochet recite?
cards.back: "…ve-tzivanu al ha-shechitah" — "Who commanded us concerning shechitah" (Yoreh Deah 19:1).

cards.front: What is shuman?
cards.back: Ordinary fat interspersed through the meat; unlike chelev, it is permitted.

cards.front: Why are the hindquarters of the carcass usually sold to non-Jews outside Israel?
cards.back: Removing the chelev and the sciatic nerve from them is difficult; in Israel this is done by specialist menakkrim.

cards.front: What should be done with meat not salted within 72 hours of shechitah?
cards.back: It can be koshered only by roasting over fire.

cards.front: Is the blood of fish forbidden by the Torah?
cards.back: No: the prohibition concerns the blood of mammals and birds.

cards.front: What meat is kosher ground meat made from?
cards.back: Only from already koshered (salted and rinsed) meat.

lessons.title: Meat and Dairy
keyIdeas: The verse "You shall not cook a kid in its mother's milk" is said three times: one may not cook such a mixture, eat it, or derive benefit from it.
By Torah law the prohibition concerns the meat of domestic cattle; the Sages extended it to birds and wild animals. Fish is not included in the prohibition.
Food is divided into basari (meat), chalavi (dairy), and parve. Hot cookware absorbs flavor, so separate meat and dairy sets are kept.
After meat, people wait: most commonly six hours, in some communities three or one. After dairy, they rinse the mouth, eat parve, and wash the hands.
Parve cooked in meat or dairy cookware takes on its status. The waiting custom is chosen together with the community rabbi.

blocks.text: The thrice-stated prohibition

blocks.ru: You shall not cook a kid in its mother's milk

blocks.text: These words appear in the Torah three times: Shemot 23:19, Shemot 34:26, and Devarim 14:21. The Oral Tradition (Chullin 115b) explains that the threefold repetition points to three separate prohibitions: **one may not cook** meat with milk together, **one may not eat** such a mixture, and **one may not derive benefit from it** — for example, selling it or feeding it to one's animal.

"Kid" in this verse is an example, not a limitation: the Torah prohibition applies to the meat of any kosher domestic animal (beef, lamb, goat meat) cooked with the milk of any kosher animal. The Sages extended the prohibition to the meat of wild animals and birds (Mishnah Chullin 8:1; according to Rabbi Akiva, 8:4, this is a decree of the Sages). Fish and locusts are not included in the prohibition: they may be eaten with milk.

The Torah does not explain the meaning of the prohibition — this is another chok. Commentators offer moral interpretations: it is impermissible to mix the source of life (milk, with which a mother feeds her young) with the death of an animal; this cultivates mercy in a person. There are also historical explanations connected with the pagan rites of antiquity.
"meat": meat, poultry, and everything cooked with them or in meat cookware. In Yiddish — "fleishik".
"dairy": milk, cheese, butter, sour cream, yogurt, and everything made with them. In Yiddish — "milchik".
"neutral": vegetables, fruits, grains, eggs, fish, water, sugar, salt. They may be eaten with either meat or dairy.
Two kitchens in one

Hot cookware absorbs the flavor of food. Therefore a kosher home has two sets of kitchenware: meat and dairy — pots, pans, plates, cutlery, cutting boards, knives, as well as sponges, towels, and drying racks. The sink is either divided (two basins) or separate tubs or racks are used. Often dishes are marked with colors — for example, red for meat and blue for dairy; this is a convenient custom, not law. Many keep a third set — for parve.

It is forbidden to place meat and dairy on one table where two people who know each other are eating, one eating meat and the other cheese, without a noticeable dividing sign (*eiker*): a separate tablecloth or placemat, or an object between the plates (Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 88).

For the same reason the Sages forbade baking bread with milk or butter unless it has an unusual shape or is baked in a very small quantity — so that it not be eaten by mistake with meat (Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 97). Therefore ordinary challah is parve.
How long to wait after meat

After a meat meal, dairy is not eaten right away. The source of the custom is the words of the Sage Mar Ukva in the Talmud (Chullin 105a): his father, after eating meat, would not eat cheese until the next day, while he himself waited until the next meal. Rambam explains the waiting by the fact that shreds of meat get stuck between the teeth; Rashi — by the fact that the fat of meat leaves an aftertaste in the mouth for a long time.

items: **6 hours** — the custom of most communities, Ashkenazi and Sephardi (Rambam; Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 89:1). Some consider it sufficient for more than five hours to pass, that is, "for the sixth hour to begin."
**3 hours** — the custom of many Jews of German origin and a number of other communities.
**1 hour** — the custom of Dutch Jews, based on the words of the Rema (Yoreh Deah 89:1): wait an hour and recite the grace after meals.

blocks.text: Usually a person follows the custom of his family. A person who has completed giyur chooses the custom together with his rabbi — most often this is the custom of the community he joins.

The count runs from the end of the meat meal to the beginning of the dairy meal. The waiting is observed also after meat dishes without meat itself (for example, potatoes stewed with meat); by widespread custom — also by children from a certain age, on the rabbi's instruction. If a person merely tasted a meat dish and spat it out, no waiting is needed, but the mouth must be rinsed.
After dairy

After dairy, meat may be eaten much sooner. It is enough to rinse the mouth, eat something neutral (for example, a piece of bread), wash the hands, and change the tablecloth and dishes (Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 89:2). Many Ashkenazim by custom wait another half an hour or an hour.

The exception is **hard aged cheese**. The Rema (Yoreh Deah 89:2) cites the custom of the strict to wait after hard cheese as long as after meat. Hard usually means cheese aged six months or more (for example, Parmesan); the specific boundaries should be clarified with a rabbi.
Parve, fish, and accidental mixtures

A parve product cooked in a meat pot takes on the status of the cookware — meat; prepared in a dairy pot — dairy. Therefore packages bear not only "parve" but also, for example, "made on dairy equipment."

Fish is not cooked or eaten together with meat — not because of the meat-and-milk prohibition, but for health reasons mentioned in the Talmud (Pesachim 76b; Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 116:2). Between fish and meat one rinses the mouth or eats a piece of bread. Ashkenazim eat fish with dairy freely (herring with sour cream), while some Sephardi communities by custom avoid this combination as well.

If a drop of milk accidentally gets into a meat dish, do not rush to throw out the food and the dishes. In many cases the rule of **bitul be-shishim** applies: an accidental admixture that makes up less than one sixtieth loses significance (Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 98). But the decision in each case is made by the rabbi — describe to him what got where, in what quantity, and whether the products were hot.

The prohibition of meat with milk is one of the most recognizable marks of the kosher way of life. Even those who keep kashrut only partially often begin with it: they do not eat cheeseburgers, do not add cream to coffee after a meat lunch.

differs.text: In Reform Judaism, the separation of meat and dairy is a personal choice. Many Reform families who observe it do not keep two sets of dishes and do not observe the waiting times; they simply do not mix meat with milk in one dish.

cards.front: Where in the Torah is "You shall not cook a kid in its mother's milk" said?
cards.back: Three times: Shemot 23:19, Shemot 34:26, Devarim 14:21.

cards.front: What three prohibitions are derived from the three repetitions?
cards.back: One may not cook meat with milk, eat such a mixture, or derive benefit from it (Chullin 115b).

cards.front: Does the prohibition apply to chicken?
cards.back: Yes, by decree of the Sages; by Torah law the prohibition applies to the meat of domestic cattle.

cards.front: May fish be eaten with dairy?
cards.back: Yes, fish is parve. Ashkenazim eat it with dairy freely; some Sephardim avoid it by custom.

cards.front: What are basari, chalavi, and parve?
cards.back: Meat, dairy, and neutral.

cards.front: Which foods are parve?
cards.back: Vegetables, fruits, grains, eggs, fish, water, sugar, salt.

cards.front: Why does a kosher kitchen have two sets of dishes?
cards.back: Hot dishes absorb flavor; meat and dairy dishes must not mix.

cards.front: Where does the custom of waiting after meat come from?
cards.back: Mar Ukva (Chullin 105a): his father waited until the next day, and he himself — until the next meal.

cards.front: How long does one wait after meat according to the Shulchan Aruch?
cards.back: 6 hours (Yoreh Deah 89:1); this is the custom of most communities.

cards.front: Who has the custom of waiting 3 hours? 1 hour?
cards.back: 3 hours — many Jews of German origin; 1 hour — the Dutch custom (according to the Rema).

cards.front: What does one do after dairy before meat?
cards.back: Rinse the mouth, eat something parve (bread), wash the hands; many Ashkenazim wait another 30–60 minutes.

cards.front: How long does one wait after hard aged cheese?
cards.back: By the custom of the strict (Rema, Yoreh Deah 89:2) — as after meat.

cards.front: Why is fish not eaten together with meat?
cards.back: For health reasons mentioned in the Talmud (Pesachim 76b; Yoreh Deah 116:2).

cards.front: What is bitul be-shishim?
cards.back: An accidental admixture of less than 1/60 loses significance; the decision in each case rests with the rabbi.

cards.front: Why is bread usually baked parve?
cards.back: The Sages forbade dairy bread of ordinary shape, so that it not be eaten with meat (Yoreh Deah 97).

cards.front: May two people eat meat and cheese at one table?
cards.back: Only with a noticeable divider (eiker): a separate tablecloth, an object between the plates (Yoreh Deah 88).

cards.front: Does the prohibition "do not cook a kid" apply only to a kid?
cards.back: No: "kid" is an example. By Torah law, the meat of any kosher domestic animal with the milk of any kosher animal is forbidden.

cards.front: What moral interpretation is given to the prohibition of meat with milk?
cards.back: One must not mix the source of life (a mother's milk) with the death of an animal; this cultivates mercy.

cards.front: How do Rambam and Rashi explain the waiting after meat?
cards.back: Rambam: shreds of meat get stuck in the teeth. Rashi: the fat of meat leaves an aftertaste in the mouth for a long time.

cards.front: What does "the sixth hour has begun" mean?
cards.back: The opinion that after meat it is sufficient for more than five hours to have passed.

cards.front: Must one wait if a meat dish was merely tasted and spat out?
cards.back: No waiting is needed, but the mouth must be rinsed.

cards.front: Does one wait after potatoes stewed with meat?
cards.back: By widespread custom — yes: one waits after meat dishes even if there is no piece of meat left on the plate.

cards.front: Red dishes for meat, blue for dairy — is this a law?
cards.back: No, a convenient custom. Many keep a third set as well — for parve.

cards.front: What happens to parve cooked in a dairy pot?
cards.back: As taught in this lesson, it takes on the dairy status of the cookware. Therefore packages may bear the note "made on dairy equipment."

lessons.title: Utensils and the Kitchen
keyIdeas: When heated, a vessel absorbs flavor. Koshering follows the rule "as it absorbed, so it expels": boiling water for what was boiled, fire for what was roasted.
The source is the purification of the Midianite vessels (Bamidbar 31:23). Methods: hagalah, iruy, libun gamur, and libun kal.
Porcelain and ceramics cannot be koshered. About glass, Sephardi and Ashkenazi customs differ; before koshering one waits 24 hours.
Metal and glass utensils from a non-Jew are immersed in a mikveh: tevilat keilim brings them into a Jewish home; it does not purge absorbed flavor.
The Sages forbade bishul akum, pat akum, chalav akum, and cheese without supervision. The kitchen is koshered before giyur together with the rabbi.

blocks.text: As it absorbed, so it expels

Any candidate must know the classical rules of utensils and koshering: this is the language of the Jewish kitchen and a subject of questions in study. How exactly you arrange your home depends on the movement and the beit din. Reform kitchen practice is discussed separately at the end of the lesson — not as a hint that "this is optional."

The laws of utensils rest on a simple observation: when heated, a vessel absorbs the flavor of food and then imparts it to other food. If treif meat was cooked in a pot, the pot itself becomes "treif," and so does everything prepared in it. Hence the main principle of koshering: **"as it absorbed, so it expels"** — a vessel is purged by the same means by which the flavor entered it: what absorbed through boiling water is koshered with boiling water; what absorbed directly through fire — by fire (Pesachim 30b).

blocks.ru: As it absorbs, so it expels

blocks.text: The source in the Torah is the account of the spoils after the war with Midian. Moshe and Elazar the kohen ordered the metal vessels to be purified: "whatever passes through fire, pass through fire, and it will be clean… and whatever does not pass through fire, pass through water."

blocks.he: כָּל דָּבָר אֲשֶׁר יָבֹא בָאֵשׁ תַּעֲבִירוּ בָאֵשׁ וְטָהֵר
blocks.translit: Kol davar asher yavo va-esh ta'aviru va-esh ve-taher
blocks.ru: Whatever passes through fire, pass through fire, and it will be clean

blocks.text: Cold contact usually does not transfer flavor: if cold cheese was placed on a clean meat plate, it is enough to wash the plate thoroughly. It is more complicated if the product was sharp (for example, if an onion was cut with a meat knife) or lay in the dish for a long time — in such cases one asks the rabbi.
Methods of koshering

items: **Hagalah** (הַגְעָלָה) — immersion in boiling water. Metal pots, cutlery, and ladles are koshered this way — that is, whatever absorbed flavor through hot liquid. After hagalah the vessel is rinsed with cold water.
**Iruy** — pouring boiling water over. Applied to metal sinks and stone or metal countertops — to surfaces on which hot liquid was poured or hot things set down.
**Libun gamur** (לִבּוּן) — heating with fire until red-hot. Grill grates, skewers, and baking sheets on which food was roasted directly over fire without liquid are koshered this way.
**Libun kal** — "light" heating: heating to the degree that paper touching the other side scorches. Used in some cases instead of hagalah, or for ovens.

blocks.text: Before koshering, the vessel is cleaned thoroughly: rust, burnt-on residue, and food remnants are removed. Usually it is not used for 24 hours (the vessel ceases to be *ben yomo* — "used the same day"): after this the absorbed flavor is considered spoiled, and koshering goes more easily.
What cannot be koshered

Earthenware, faience, and porcelain cannot be koshered: the Torah speaks of an earthenware vessel in which the meat of a sacrifice was cooked, saying that it must be broken (Vayikra 6:21) — hence clay does not give back what it absorbed. About **glass** customs differ. According to the Shulchan Aruch (Orach Chaim 451:26), glass does not absorb at all, and it is enough to wash it — this is what many Sephardim do. The Rema writes in the same place that Ashkenazim do not kosher glass (at least for Pesach). For plastic, Teflon, enamel, and ceramic cooktops opinions differ, so their status should be clarified with a rabbi.

Koshering a kitchen is serious work: the oven, the stove, the sink, the dishwasher, and the microwave are koshered by separate rules. Before giyur the kitchen is usually koshered together with a rabbi or an experienced member of the community. Some of the old dishes will have to be replaced — that is cheaper and more reliable.
Tevilat keilim — immersion of dishes

Metal dishes for food, made by or bought from a non-Jew, are immersed in a mikveh or a natural source (a river, the sea, a spring) before first use. This is a mitzvah — **tevilat keilim**; it is derived from the same passage about the vessels of Midyan (Bamidbar 31:23; Avodah Zarah 75b). Immersion does not purify a vessel from a non-kosher taste — it is done even with brand-new dishes; it is as if it transfers the item "into holiness" of a Jewish home. Glass dishes are immersed by enactment of the sages, because glass, like metal, can be re-melted (Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 120; Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 37).

items: First the dishes are washed and the stickers and glue are removed: nothing must come between the water and the surface.
The item is immersed fully, in one motion, so that the water touches all of its surfaces; it is held loosely, not squeezed.
Before the immersion a blessing is said: for one item — "al tevilat keli", for several — "al tevilat keilim".

Wooden, plastic, and paper dishes and unglazed clay are, by the basic rule, not immersed; regarding glazed ceramics, disposable aluminum dishes, and electrical appliances customs differ — with no blessing, or with no immersion at all.

blocks.he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם אֲשֶׁר קִדְּשָׁנוּ בְּמִצְוֹתָיו וְצִוָּנוּ עַל טְבִילַת כְּלִי
blocks.translit: Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu melech ha'olam, asher kidshanu bemitzvotav, vetzivanu al tevilat keli
blocks.ru: Blessed are You, L-rd our G-d, King of the universe, who sanctified us with His mitzvot and commanded us concerning the immersion of a vessel

blocks.text: Food prepared by a non-Jew

The sages instituted several prohibitions on food that in itself consists of kosher ingredients but is prepared by a non-Jew. Their purpose is to preserve the separateness of the Jewish community and to prevent intermarriage, as well as to guard against mistakes in kashrut (Avodah Zarah 35b–38a).

items: **Bishul akum** (בִּשּׁוּל עַכּוּ״ם, "cooked by a non-Jew"; Yoreh Deah 113). The prohibition concerns dishes that are not eaten raw and that are worthy of a "royal table" (for example, meat, fish, eggs, potatoes). For food to count as "bishul Yisrael", a Jew must take part in the cooking: by Ashkenazi custom (Rema) it is enough for a Jew to light the fire; by Sephardi custom (Shulchan Aruch) — that he himself put the food on the fire or stirred it. That is why in kosher restaurants the fire is lit by the mashgiach.

**Pat akum** (Yoreh Deah 112). Bread baked by a non-Jew at home is forbidden. Bread from a bakery (*pat palter*) with kosher ingredients many authorities permit when there is no Jewish-baked bread (*pat Yisrael*). During the Ten Days of Repentance even those who are lenient in this customarily eat only pat Yisrael (Orach Chaim 603:1).

**Chalav akum** (Yoreh Deah 115). Milk milked without a Jew present was prohibited by the sages for fear of admixture of milk from non-kosher animals. Some authorities (in particular, R. Moshe Feinstein) permitted milk under strict government supervision, but many observe **chalav Yisrael**.
**Gevinat akum** — cheese made without Jewish supervision is forbidden, in particular because of rennet from the stomachs of animals not slaughtered according to kashrut.

blocks.text: Masorti (Conservative Judaism) requires a kosher kitchen with separate dishes and recognizes the laws of koshering; many Conservative communities also practice tevilat keilim. Positions on bishul akum, pat akum, and cheese are more lenient than the Orthodox ones — they should be clarified with the community rabbi.
The kitchen in a Reform home

Reform Judaism does not consider obligatory two sets of dishes, separate sinks, tevilat keilim, and full koshering of a kitchen according to the rules of the Shulchan Aruch. This does not mean that the topic of kashrut is empty for a progressive Jew or "written on a leftover basis". Kashrut is understood as a discipline of holiness, ethics, and belonging to the people: a person studies the laws, understands their meaning, and consciously takes upon himself the measure he is ready to keep honestly.

In practice many Reform families begin with clear, steady steps: they do not eat the animals forbidden by the Torah (pork, seafood without scales and fins), they separate meat and dairy at least at the table or in time, they look for ethically acceptable meat, and they reduce cruelty and wastefulness. Some, over time, acquire separate dishes or a fully kosher kitchen — as a personal path, not as a condition of "real" Jewishness. Some keep a stricter order at home and a freer one outside it. The main thing is not to confuse ignorance with choice and not to pass off convenience as principle.

In progressive communities people increasingly speak also of **ethical kashrut**: working conditions, ecology, treatment of animals, eating habits that do not debase the image of G-d in man and in the world. This is not a replacement for the Torah's mitzvot about permitted animals, but an additional layer of responsibility. In the giyur school of the Russian Union of Progressive Jewish Communities (ROOPI), kashrut is usually included in the program; specific home requirements are clarified by the community rabbi.

At a Reform beit din you are more likely to be asked: what exactly do you eat and not eat, how your kitchen is arranged, what changed over the year of study, and why you chose this order. "I observe nothing because in Reform you may" is a weak answer. "I studied the laws, in our family we keep this, and this is where I am heading" is a strong and honest one.

cards.front: What is the main principle of koshering dishes?
cards.back: "As it absorbed, so it gives off" (kevole'o kach polto): a vessel is purged by the same means by which the taste entered it.

cards.front: Where in the Torah is the source of the laws of koshering dishes?
cards.back: The vessels taken from Midyan: "through fire… through water" (Bamidbar 31:21–23).

cards.front: What is hag'alah?
cards.back: Koshering by immersion in boiling water — for metal pots and utensils.

cards.front: What is libun gamur?
cards.back: Heating until red-hot in fire — for grill grates, skewers, and baking trays.

cards.front: What is iruy?
cards.back: Pouring boiling water over — for sinks and countertops.

cards.front: Can porcelain and ceramic be koshered?
cards.back: No: earthenware does not release what it absorbed (Vayikra 6:21).

cards.front: How do Sephardim and Ashkenazim regard the koshering of glass?
cards.back: Shulchan Aruch: glass does not absorb, washing suffices; Rema: Ashkenazim do not kosher glass (OC 451:26).

cards.front: What does "ben yomo" mean?
cards.back: A vessel used within the last 24 hours; before koshering one usually waits a day.

cards.front: Which dishes must be immersed in a mikveh (tevilat keilim)?
cards.back: Metal and glass dishes for food, made by or purchased from a non-Jew.

cards.front: What blessing is said when immersing a single item?
cards.back: "…vetzivanu al tevilat keli"; for several — "al tevilat keilim".

cards.front: Must wooden and plastic dishes be immersed?
cards.back: By the basic rule — no.

cards.front: What is bishul akum?
cards.back: Food prepared by a non-Jew, if it is not eaten raw and is worthy of a "royal table" (Yoreh Deah 113).

cards.front: How is food made "bishul Yisrael"?
cards.back: Ashkenazim: a Jew lights the fire; Sephardim: a Jew puts the food on the fire or takes part in the cooking.

cards.front: What is pat palter?
cards.back: Bread from a non-Jewish bakery with kosher ingredients; many permit it when there is no pat Yisrael.

cards.front: When do even those lenient toward pat palter eat only pat Yisrael?
cards.back: During the Ten Days of Repentance (Orach Chaim 603:1).

cards.front: What is chalav Yisrael?
cards.back: Milk milked in the presence of a Jew (Yoreh Deah 115).

cards.front: Are plastic, Teflon, and enamel koshered?
cards.back: Authorities' opinions differ, so the status of such dishes is clarified with a rabbi.

cards.front: What is libun kal?
cards.back: "Light" heating: heating at which paper held against the other side scorches; sometimes done instead of hag'alah, or for ovens.

cards.front: What is done with a dish immediately after hag'alah?
cards.back: It is rinsed in cold water.

cards.front: When does even cold contact with a dish require asking a rabbi?
cards.back: If the food is sharp (an onion cut with a meat knife) or lay in the dish for a long time.

cards.front: How is a dish properly immersed in a mikveh?
cards.back: Remove the stickers and glue, immerse it fully in one motion, holding it loosely, so that the water touches all of its surfaces.

cards.front: Does tevilat keilim purify from a non-kosher taste?
cards.back: No: it is done even with new dishes; it brings the item into the holiness of a Jewish home.

cards.front: Why is cheese without Jewish supervision (gevinat akum) forbidden?
cards.back: In particular because of rennet from the stomachs of animals not slaughtered according to kashrut.

cards.front: Why did the sages prohibit food prepared by a non-Jew?
cards.back: To preserve the community's separateness, prevent intermarriage, and guard against mistakes in kashrut (Avodah Zarah 35b–38a).

lessons.title: Hechsher, wine, and kashrut across the movements
keyIdeas: Processed foods need a hechsher: they can contain gelatin, carmine, whey, wine, and shared production lines with non-kosher products.
Read the symbol by the organization (OU, badatz, and others) and by the markings: D — dairy, P — kosher for Pesach. A single letter K is not reliable.
Wine for kiddush is special: yayin nesech and stam yeynam are forbidden; mevushal does not become prohibited through a non-Jew's touch.
For the Orthodox, kashrut is obligatory in full; Masorti considers it halacha but is more lenient on particulars. For Reform Jews it is a personal choice.
As a guest of those who do not observe kashrut, act tactfully: your own food, disposable dishes, products with a hechsher — without humiliating relatives.

blocks.text: Why a hechsher is needed

A hundred years ago the housewife herself knew what her dinner was made of. Today a pack of cookies can contain dozens of ingredients: gelatin (usually from pig skin or the bones of animals not slaughtered according to kashrut), glycerin and emulsifiers of animal origin, carmine from insects, whey (dairy!), wine or grape juice, flavorings of unknown composition. In addition, a kosher product may be made on the same line as a non-kosher one. That is why processed foods need a **hechsher** — certification from a kashrut organization that has checked the recipe, the raw materials, and the production.
"permission": a kashrut certificate and a mark on the packaging attesting that the product is kosher under the supervision of a particular organization or rabbi.
"overseer": a kashrut specialist who supervises a production facility, a restaurant, or a kitchen.
How to read the labeling

items: **OU** (the letter U in a circle) — the Orthodox Union (USA), one of the largest kashrut systems in the world.
**OK** (the letter K in a circle), **Star-K** (a K in a star) — large American organizations.
**KLBD** — kashrut of the London beit din (United Kingdom).
**Badatz** (בד״ץ, "beit din tzedek") — supervision by rabbinical courts, usually strict; for example, the Badatz of the Eda HaChareidit in Jerusalem.
In Israel — certificates of the Chief Rabbinate and of local rabbinates; "mehadrin" means a higher level of stringency.
In Russia and the CIS countries kashrut is certified by the rabbinates of major Jewish organizations; they also publish lists of checked products from ordinary stores.
**D**, Dairy, חָלָבִי — dairy; **DE** — made on dairy equipment.
**M**, Meat, בְּשָׂרִי — meat.
**Pareve**, פַּרְוֶה — neutral.
**P** next to the symbol or “כָּשֵׁר לְפֶסַח” — kosher for Pesach. Attention: here “P” does not mean “pareve”!

blocks.text: A single letter "K" on the packaging is not a protected mark: any manufacturer can print it. Look at which organization stands behind the symbol. Different communities recognize different hechshers — ask your rabbi which ones may be relied upon.
Wine: a special case
Wine in Jewish life is not just a drink. Kiddush and havdalah are said over it, it is drunk at weddings and brit milah, and the four cups at the Pesach seder. That is why wine has its own blessing.

blocks.he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם בּוֹרֵא פְּרִי הַגָּפֶן
blocks.translit: Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu melech ha'olam, borei pri hagafen
blocks.ru: Blessed are You, L-rd our G-d, King of the universe, who creates the fruit of the vine

blocks.text: In ancient times wine was poured out as a libation to idols. Wine intended for idol worship — **yayin nesech** — is forbidden by the Torah (tradition connects the prohibition with Devarim 32:38). The sages extended the prohibition to **stam yeynam** — any wine produced by a non-Jew, as well as kosher wine that a non-Jew touched or moved in an open vessel — in order to distance Jews from idol worship and from closeness that leads to intermarriage (Avodah Zarah 29b, 36b; Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 123). The prohibition extends to grape juice, and also to cognac and brandy made from grapes.

That is why kosher wine — from the grape harvest to the sealing of the bottle — is handled only by Jews who observe Shabbat. The exception is **mevushal** wine ("boiled"; today, pasteurized): according to halacha it does not become forbidden if a non-Jew touches it (Yoreh Deah 123:3). That is why at banquets and in restaurants, where wine is poured by non-Jewish waiters, mevushal is served. Opinions differ about the temperature required for the heating. In Israel, products of vegetable origin are additionally checked for compliance with the agricultural mitzvot — terumot and maasrot, orlah, and shemittah.
Kashrut in practice

A kosher restaurant must display a valid certificate (*teudat kashrut*) with a date and the name of the organization. As a guest in the home of friends who do not observe kashrut, you may respectfully offer to bring your own food, eat on disposable dishes, or limit yourself to fresh fruit and packaged products with a hechsher. When traveling, kosher stores, community centers, and product lists help. It is important to remember tact: kashrut must not become an occasion to humiliate relatives who do not observe it. If your parents are not Jewish, explain to them why you act this way, and together find a way to preserve family meals.
Orthodox Judaism

For Orthodox Judaism, kashrut is obligatory halacha in its fullness: both the laws of the Torah and the enactments of the sages. A giyur candidate must run a fully kosher home, buy only products with a recognized hechsher, and know the laws of meat and dairy, checking products, and koshering dishes. The beit din asks about kashrut in detail, and sometimes a mentor or rabbi comes to see how the kitchen is arranged.
Conservative Judaism (Masorti)

The Conservative movement considers kashrut obligatory halacha. Its decisions are made by the Committee on Jewish Law and Standards (CJLS) of the Rabbinical Assembly. Community members are expected to keep a kosher home: meat only from shechitah, separate dishes, abstaining from forbidden products. On a number of particular questions the CJLS has adopted more lenient rulings than the Orthodox authorities — for example, on wine made by non-Jews and on certain cheeses. In practice, many Conservative Jews eat dairy or vegetarian food in non-kosher restaurants away from home; the movement does not consider this ideal. Masorti also pays attention to the ethics of food production: in the 2000s the movement launched the "Magen Tzedek" initiative — an ethical mark in addition to the hechsher.

differs.text: The Conservative movement (CJLS) does not apply the prohibition of stam yeynam to wine produced by non-Jews without idolatrous rites, and is more lenient than the Orthodox on questions of cheeses and food prepared by non-Jews.

blocks.text: Reform Judaism

Early American Reform Judaism declared the laws of food non-obligatory, born of an era alien to modernity, in the Pittsburgh Platform of 1885. Later the approach changed: the "Principles of Reform Judaism" of 1999 call for studying the mitzvot and fulfilling those that sanctify life, and the Central Conference of American Rabbis (CCAR) published a book on Jewish food ethics, "The Sacred Table" (2011). Today Reform Judaism regards kashrut as a **conscious personal choice**.

items: Many Reform Jews observe "Torah kashrut": they do not eat pork and seafood.
Many do not mix meat with milk, especially at home or at community events.
"Ethical kashrut": care for animals (tzaar baalei chaim), fair labor for workers, ecology, rejection of wastefulness; some people become vegetarians for these reasons.

In Reform giyur schools (for example, in progressive Jewish communities in Russia) the candidate studies the traditional laws and, together with a rabbi, decides which practices to adopt in his or her life.

differs.text: A Reform rabbi does not require a kosher kitchen from the candidate; the candidate is expected to know the laws of kashrut and to have a well-considered personal decision about how to observe them.

blocks.text: At any beit din you may be asked: "What does kashrut mean to you?" Answer honestly, based on what you actually do, and explain how kashrut is connected for you with holiness, discipline, and belonging to the Jewish people.

A conscious choice here is not a synonym for arbitrariness. Reform rabbis ask the candidate to know the classical categories (permitted animals, blood, meat and dairy, hechsher), to be able to explain why the Jewish tradition connects food with holiness at all, and to show an already living practice, not only the intention "someday". The measure of expectations differs from country to country: in some North American communities the emphasis is on study and ethics, while ROOPI communities and many Israeli progressive communities treat home kashrut more attentively. Always ask your rabbi, and speak his language, not a borrowed one.

questions.prompt: What does the word “kosher” literally mean?
options: Pure
Fit, suitable
Holy
Permitted by the sages
questions.explanation: The root כ-ש-ר means “fit, suitable”; this is what everything that is fit according to halacha is called.

questions.prompt: In which chapters of the Torah are the main signs of permitted animals set out?
options: Bereshit 1 and Shemot 12
Vayikra 11 and Devarim 14
Shemot 20 and Devarim 5
Vayikra 19 and Bamidbar 15
questions.explanation: The signs of animals and fish, the list of birds and insects — in Vayikra 11 and Devarim 14:3–21.

questions.prompt: To which category of mitzvot do the sages assign most of the laws of kashrut?
options: Mishpatim — laws intelligible to reason
Edot — commandments that testify
Chukim — decrees without explanation in the Torah
Mitzvot given to all descendants of Noah
questions.explanation: The Torah does not explain the reasons for kashrut, so it is considered the classic example of a chok.

questions.prompt: Which food prohibition is binding on non-Jews as well (descendants of Noah)?
options: The prohibition of pork
The prohibition of meat with milk
The prohibition of a limb from a living animal (eiver min ha-chai)
The prohibition of the blood of fish
questions.explanation: Of the food laws, only the prohibition of eiver min ha-chai was given to the descendants of Noah.

questions.prompt: In the Guide for the Perplexed, Rambam explained forbidden food, among other things, by harm to health.
questions.explanation: Rambam gives a medical explanation, though other authors (for example, Abarbanel) disputed it.

questions.prompt: According to Sifre, the ideal Jew should feel disgust at pork.
questions.explanation: On the contrary: one should say “I would like to, but my Father in Heaven has forbidden it” — observance for the sake of the mitzvah, not out of disgust.

questions.prompt: Match the term and its meaning.
questions.explanation: These are the basic terms of the section on kashrut.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the section of the Shulchan Aruch that collects the laws of kashrut?
questions.explanation: The Shulchan Aruch is divided into four parts; the laws of food are in Yoreh Deah.

questions.prompt: A member of the beit din asks: “The Torah does not explain the reasons for kashrut. Why do you observe it?” Answer.
questions.modelAnswer: Kashrut is a chok, a commandment-decree, and I observe it above all because the Almighty commanded it, not because of taste or diet; the Sifra teaches us to say: “I would like to, but my Father in Heaven has forbidden it.” The Torah itself connects the laws of food with holiness: “Sanctify yourselves and be holy, for I am holy” (Vayikra 11:44). The commentators saw in kashrut the training of character and self-discipline: every meal becomes a choice. Kashrut connects me with the Jewish people, makes my home open to any Jew, and my table a likeness of the altar.
keyPoints: Kashrut is a chok, performed as a mitzvah
Sifra: “I want to, but my Father in Heaven has forbidden it”
Holiness (Vayikra 11:44)
Discipline and character
Bond with the people, a kosher home, the table as an altar
questions.explanation: The beit din checks whether the candidate understands the religious meaning of kashrut.

questions.prompt: Which animal has split hooves but does not chew the cud, and is therefore forbidden?
options: Camel
Hare
Pig
Hyrax
questions.explanation: The pig is the only one of the four animals named by the Torah that has split hooves but does not chew the cud.

questions.prompt: Which of these fish is non-kosher?
options: Carp
Salmon
Catfish
Herring
questions.explanation: The catfish has no scales, so it is forbidden; carp, salmon and herring are kosher.

questions.prompt: Why do we eat only birds that have a mesorah (tradition)?
options: The Torah gives only one sign for birds
The names of the forbidden birds in the Torah cannot always be reliably identified
All birds except the chicken are forbidden by the Torah
Birds do not require shechitah
questions.explanation: The Torah lists the forbidden birds, but their identification is uncertain, so people rely on tradition.
questions.source: Mishnah Chullin 3:6; Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 82:2 (Rema)

questions.prompt: Why is honey kosher even though the bee is a non-kosher insect?
options: Honey is pareve
The bee is not on the list of forbidden insects
Honey is not produced by the bee's body; it is only gathered by it
Honey is permitted only in Israel
questions.explanation: The Talmud explains that honey is flower nectar merely stored in the bee's body.

questions.prompt: Which method of checking leafy greens for insects is common in Orthodox homes?
options: It is enough to boil the greens
Soak them in water with detergent, rinse under running water and inspect in the light
Check one leaf from the bunch
Salt them and leave for an hour
questions.explanation: Insects visible to the eye are forbidden, so greens are soaked, rinsed and inspected.

questions.prompt: Every fish that has scales also has fins.
questions.explanation: So says the Mishnah, so in practice the scales are checked.

questions.prompt: Mare's milk is permitted because milk is not meat.
questions.explanation: The products of non-kosher animals are forbidden: “what comes from the impure is impure.”

questions.prompt: Match the product and its status.
questions.explanation: The signs of kashrut differ for mammals, fish and birds.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the unbroken tradition on the basis of which a particular bird is considered kosher?
questions.explanation: Without a mesorah a bird is not eaten, even if it seems suitable by its signs.

questions.prompt: Explain how to determine whether a mammal, a fish and a bird are kosher. Give examples.
questions.modelAnswer: A mammal is kosher if it has split hooves and chews the cud — both signs are needed (Vayikra 11:3); therefore the cow, sheep and goat are permitted, while the pig, camel and hare are not. A fish is kosher if it has fins and scales that can be removed (Vayikra 11:9): salmon and carp are permitted, while catfish, eel and all seafood are not. For birds the Torah lists the forbidden species, and in practice only birds with a tradition (mesorah) are eaten: chicken, turkey, duck, goose. In addition, meat and poultry are kosher only after shechitah and the removal of the blood.
keyPoints: Two signs for mammals
Fins and scales for fish
Birds — by mesorah
Examples of permitted and forbidden
Shechitah is needed
questions.explanation: Basic knowledge checked at every beit din.

options: From the words “as I have commanded you” (Devarim 12:21)
From the story of Avraham's offering
From the prohibition of gid ha-nashe
From the laws of Pesach
questions.explanation: The method of slaughter is not described in the Written Torah, but it says “as I have commanded you.”
