Very sharp, with an absolutely smooth blade
Necessarily new for each animal
Made of stone, as in ancient times
questions.explanation: The slightest nick makes the shechitah invalid, so the knife is checked before and after slaughter.

questions.prompt: Why is the sciatic nerve (gid ha-nashe) forbidden?
options: It is harmful to health
In memory of Yaakov's struggle with the angel
It was brought on the altar
Because of the prohibition of blood
questions.explanation: The Torah directly connects the prohibition with the injury to Yaakov's hip.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the five violations that render shechitah invalid?
options: Shegiyah — pausing
Derasah — pressing
Chaladah — concealing the knife
Melichah — salting
questions.explanation: Melichah is the removal of blood after shechitah, not a violation; the fifth violation is hagramah or ikur.

questions.prompt: The prohibition of chelev applies to the meat of chicken and deer.
questions.explanation: Chelev is forbidden only in domestic cattle — the ox, sheep and goat.

questions.prompt: Liver is koshered by ordinary salting, like the rest of the meat.
questions.explanation: Because of its abundance of blood, liver is koshered only by roasting over fire.

questions.prompt: Match the term and its meaning.
questions.explanation: Key concepts of the lesson on shechitah.
questions.source: Vayikra 7:23; Bereshit 32:33; Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 39

questions.prompt: What is the name, in Yiddish, for meat from an animal with completely smooth lungs, without adhesions?
questions.explanation: “Glatt” means smooth; Sephardim eat only such meat (according to the Beit Yosef).

questions.prompt: What is the correct order of salting meat?
options: Salt it, soak for half an hour, rinse
Soak for half an hour, salt on all sides, leave for an hour, rinse
Salt with fine salt and cook at once
Freeze, then salt and rinse once
questions.explanation: Soaking, salting for an hour on a rack and thorough rinsing — this is the basic order of melichah.
questions.source: Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 36; Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 69

questions.prompt: Why does a kosher breed of animal still not make the meat kosher? List what must happen before the meat reaches the table.
questions.modelAnswer: A kosher animal must be slaughtered by shechitah: a trained shochet makes a quick, continuous cut with a smooth knife; otherwise the meat is considered nevelah. After the shechitah the organs, especially the lungs, are checked: an animal with a serious defect is treif. Then the forbidden fat (chelev) and the sciatic nerve (gid ha-nashe) are removed. Finally the blood is removed by salting or roasting, because the Torah forbids blood: “the blood is the life.” Therefore meat is bought only with a reliable hechsher.
keyPoints: Shechitah by a trained shochet
Checking for treifot
Removal of chelev and gid ha-nashe
Removal of blood (salting)
Buy with a hechsher
questions.explanation: The candidate must understand the whole chain by which kosher meat is produced.
questions.source: Devarim 12:21–23; Vayikra 7:23; Bereshit 32:33; Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 36

questions.prompt: How many times does the Torah repeat the prohibition “do not cook a kid in its mother's milk”?
options: Once
Twice
Three times
Seven times
questions.explanation: Shemot 23:19, Shemot 34:26 and Devarim 14:21; from this three prohibitions are derived.

questions.prompt: Which three prohibitions are derived from the threefold repetition of the verse?
options: Cooking, eating and deriving benefit
Cooking, frying and salting
Eating, selling and storing in one refrigerator
Cooking, eating and looking
questions.explanation: It is forbidden to cook meat with milk, to eat such a mixture and to derive benefit from it.

questions.prompt: Which product is pareve?
options: Butter
Chicken broth
Egg
Cheese
questions.explanation: The eggs of kosher birds are a neutral food; butter and cheese are dairy, broth is meat.

questions.prompt: Which waiting period after meat is accepted by most communities according to the Shulchan Aruch?
options: 1 hour
3 hours
6 hours
24 hours
questions.explanation: Six hours — the opinion of Rambam and the Shulchan Aruch; 3 and 1 hour are customs of individual communities.

questions.prompt: According to the Torah, the prohibition of meat with milk also applies to fish.
questions.explanation: Fish is pareve; the Mishnah explicitly excludes fish and locusts.

questions.prompt: The prohibition of eating chicken with milk was instituted by the sages, not directly by the Torah.
questions.explanation: By Torah law the prohibition concerns the meat of domestic cattle; the sages extended it to birds and wild animals.

questions.prompt: Match the waiting custom after meat and the community.
questions.explanation: Customs differ; a person follows the custom of his family or community.
questions.source: Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 89:1 and Rema ad loc.

questions.prompt: What is the Hebrew name for neutral food — neither meat nor dairy?
questions.explanation: Pareve can be eaten with both meat and dairy.

questions.prompt: A drop of milk falls into a pot of hot meat soup. What is the right thing to do?
options: Throw out the soup and the pot at once
Do nothing: a drop does not count
Consult a rabbi, saying how much milk fell into what volume
Add more meat so the mixture becomes meat
questions.explanation: Often the rule of 1/60 (bitul be-shishim) applies, but the decision is made by the rabbi; deliberately “diluting” a prohibition is not allowed.

questions.prompt: Describe how a kosher home separates meat and dairy — in the kitchen and at the table.
questions.modelAnswer: In a kosher home there are two sets of dishes — meat and dairy: pots, pans, plates, cutlery, cutting boards, as well as sponges and towels; they are often marked with colors. The sink is divided or separate basins are used. Meat and dairy are not cooked or eaten together, and pareve products take on the status of the dishes in which they were prepared. After meat one waits before dairy — by custom six, three or one hour; after dairy one rinses the mouth, eats something neutral and washes the hands. Fish and eggs, being pareve, can be eaten with any food, although fish is not eaten together with meat.
keyPoints: Two sets of dishes
Separate sink/sponges
Waiting after meat according to custom
What to do after dairy
Pareve status
questions.explanation: A practical question about how the candidate runs his kitchen.

questions.prompt: How is a metal pot in which non-kosher soup was cooked koshered?
options: Libun gamur — by heating until red-hot
Hagalah — by immersion in boiling water
With cold water and soap
It cannot be koshered
questions.explanation: The pot absorbed flavor through a hot liquid, so it is koshered with boiling water.

questions.prompt: Which dishes cannot be koshered under any conditions?
options: Stainless steel
Silver spoons
Porcelain and ceramic dishes
Cast-iron grill grate
questions.explanation: Earthenware does not give up what it has absorbed (Vayikra 6:21).

questions.prompt: Which utensils bought in an ordinary store must be immersed in a mikveh before use?
options: Wooden cutting board
Metal pot
Plastic container
Paper plates
questions.explanation: Tevilat keilim is obligatory for metal (and, by rabbinic decree, glass) utensils from a non-Jew.
questions.source: Bamidbar 31:23; Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 120; Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 37

questions.prompt: According to the Ashkenazi custom (Rema), what is sufficient for food cooked by a non-Jewish cook not to count as bishul akum?
options: A Jew must taste the dish
A Jew must light the fire
A Jew must buy the ingredients
Nothing: bishul akum does not apply to Ashkenazim
questions.explanation: According to the Rema it is enough for a Jew to light the fire; according to the Shulchan Aruch a Jew must place the food on the fire.
questions.source: Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 113:7 and Rema ad loc.

questions.prompt: According to the Shulchan Aruch (the custom of many Sephardim), glass dishes need only a thorough washing, while according to the Ashkenazi Rema glass cannot be koshered.
questions.explanation: This is a classic example of the difference between Ashkenazi and Sephardi customs.
questions.source: Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 451:26 and Rema ad loc.

questions.prompt: Tevilat keilim is needed only for old utensils in which non-kosher food was cooked.
questions.explanation: New utensils are also immersed: this is not a cleansing from absorbed flavor, but a separate mitzvah.
questions.source: Avodah Zarah 75b; Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 120

questions.prompt: Match the item and the method of koshering.
questions.explanation: The principle: “as it absorbed, so it gives out.”
questions.source: Pesachim 30b; Vayikra 6:21; Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 451

questions.prompt: You are about to kosher your kitchen before giyur. Tell how you will proceed.
questions.modelAnswer: I will do it together with a rabbi or an experienced member of the community. First I will scrub everything thoroughly and not use for 24 hours the utensils I want to kosher. Metal pots and cutlery I will kosher by hagalah — immersion in boiling water; grates and baking sheets by heating (libun); the sink and countertops by pouring boiling water over them. Porcelain and ceramics, which cannot be koshered, I will replace, and about glass and plastic I will ask the rabbi. Then I will set up separate sets for meat and dairy and, as instructed by the rabbi, immerse the new metal and glass utensils in the mikveh.
keyPoints: With a rabbi
Cleaning and 24 hours
Hagalah, libun, iruy
Replacing ceramics
Separate sets, tevilat keilim
questions.explanation: The beit din wants to see that the candidate understands practice, not only theory.
questions.source: Bamidbar 31:21–23; Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 451; Yoreh Deah 120–121

differs.text: In Reform practice, fully koshering the kitchen and two sets of dishes are usually not required. Tell what order of food and dishes you already keep, what of the classical laws you know, and what standard you consciously take upon yourself. If you are just now setting up a stricter kitchen — describe the steps in your own words.

questions.prompt: What does the letter “P” next to the kashrut symbol on an American product mean?
options: Parve
Kosher for Pesach
Product under rabbinical supervision
Has been pasteurized
questions.explanation: “P” stands for Passover; pareve is written as the word “Pareve”.
questions.source: Labeling of OU and other kashrut agencies

questions.prompt: Why is mevushal wine served at banquets with non-Jewish waiters?
options: It is cheaper
It does not become forbidden through a non-Jew's touch
It is non-alcoholic
No blessing is needed over it
questions.explanation: Cooked (pasteurized) wine is not subject to the prohibition of stam yayinam.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the position of the Conservative movement (Masorti)?
options: Kashrut is a personal choice without obligations
Kashrut is binding halacha; decisions are made by the CJLS, and in private matters it is more lenient than the Orthodox
Kashrut is obligatory only in Israel
Conservatives recognize only the laws of kashrut written in the Torah
questions.explanation: Masorti considers halacha, including kashrut, binding and interprets it through the Committee on Jewish Law and Standards.
questions.source: Rabbinical Assembly / CJLS; overview of the movement (Derakhim)

questions.prompt: The letter “K” on a package by itself is a reliable guarantee of kashrut.
questions.explanation: “K” is not a protected mark; what matters is which organization stands behind the symbol.
questions.source: Practice of kashrut organizations (OU, OK, Star-K)

questions.prompt: What is the certificate or symbol certifying a product's kashrut called?
questions.explanation: A hechsher is issued by an organization or a rabbi who supervise the production.

questions.prompt: How does Reform Judaism approach kashrut, and what have you decided to do yourself?
questions.modelAnswer: Early Reform Judaism (the Pittsburgh Platform of 1885) declared the laws of food non-binding. Today Reform Judaism sees kashrut as a conscious personal choice: having studied the tradition, a person decides which practices will make his life holy. Many do not eat pork and seafood, do not mix meat with milk, and also keep “ethical kashrut” — concern for animals, honest labor and the environment. I, for example, have decided not to eat the animals forbidden by the Torah and not to mix meat with dairy at home, because this connects me with the Jewish people.
keyPoints: Pittsburgh 1885 — non-bindingness
Conscious choice after study
Torah kashrut, meat/dairy
Ethical kashrut
A personal decision with justification
questions.explanation: A Reform beit din expects a considered personal answer.
questions.source: Pittsburgh Platform (1885); “Principles of Reform Judaism” (1999); reformspb.ru/giura

questions.prompt: Explain what stam yayinam is and why kosher wine is made only by Jews who observe Shabbat.
questions.modelAnswer: The Torah forbids yayin nesach — wine poured out to idols. The sages extended the prohibition to stam yayinam — any wine made by a non-Jew or touched by him while open — in order to keep Jews away from idolatry and from socializing that leads to intermarriage. Therefore kosher wine is produced, from the pressing of the grapes to the sealing of the bottles, by Jews who observe Shabbat. Mevushal (pasteurized) wine does not become forbidden through a non-Jew's touch, so it is served where waiters pour. The prohibition also applies to grape juice and brandy.
keyPoints: Yayin nesach — Torah prohibition
Stam yayinam — rabbinic decree
Reasons: idolatry and intermarriage
Production by observant Jews
Mevushal
questions.explanation: An Orthodox beit din often asks about wine for kiddush.
questions.source: Avodah Zarah 29b, 36b; Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 123

questions.prompt: Your relatives, who do not keep kashrut, have invited you to a family dinner. What will you do?
questions.modelAnswer: In advance, and with respect, I will explain that I keep kashrut and why it matters to me, so that no one is offended. I will offer to bring my own food or kosher products with a hechsher; I can eat off disposable dishes, as well as fresh fruit and vegetables and sealed kosher products. The main thing is to preserve warm relations with my family: kashrut must not become a cause of conflict or arrogance. If anything is unclear, I will consult my rabbi.
keyPoints: Explain in advance, tactfully
Own food / disposable dishes
Products with a hechsher
Respect for the family
A rabbi's advice
questions.explanation: The beit din checks how the candidate will combine kashrut with family life.
questions.source: R. Ch. Donin, “To Be a Jew,” chapter on kashrut; ru.chabad.org — articles on kashrut

questions.prompt: How will kashrut enter your everyday life? If your home is not yet fully kosher, where will you begin?
questions.modelAnswer: For me, kashrut is not a diet and not a matter of taste, but a mitzvah: I give up certain foods because the Almighty so commanded, not because I find them repugnant. While I am preparing for giyur, this is learning; after giyur, the laws of food will become an obligation. Together with my mentor I will start with a clear step: not eating pork, seafood, and other clearly forbidden foods, then separating meat from dairy. Next I will move on to products with a hechsher and, when I am ready, I will kasher the kitchen with a rabbi. Thus every meal will become a choice and a part of the holiness of which the Torah speaks.
keyPoints: Kashrut is a chok, a mitzvah of the Almighty, not a diet or an aversion
Before giyur it is preparation; after giyur it is an obligation
Order: forbidden animals, then meat and dairy, hechsher, kitchen
A meal is bound up with holiness
questions.explanation: The beit din looks to see whether the candidate has an honest, workable plan, not just knowledge of definitions.

differs.text: In Reform Judaism kashrut is not obligatory: the candidate describes a thoughtful personal choice made after studying the tradition, rather than a complete transition to a kosher kitchen as a duty.

questions.prompt: As a guest you are offered pork, shrimp, and fish fillet without skin. What will you choose, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: I will not take the pork: a pig has cloven hooves but does not chew the cud, and the Torah requires both signs at once. I will not take the shrimp either: they have neither fins nor scales, like other seafood. Fish fillet without skin I cannot check, so I will decline it or ask for a whole fish, with skin or with a reliable hechsher — so the scales are visible, as on salmon or carp. It is important to me to be able to apply the signs to ordinary food, not just to recite them.
keyPoints: The pig has only one of the two signs and is forbidden
Seafood without fins and scales is forbidden
Fillet without skin cannot be checked: skin, a whole fish, or a hechsher is needed
The answer rests on the Torah's signs, not on taste
questions.explanation: The beit din checks whether the candidate can apply the signs of kashrut to real food.

differs.text: In Reform Judaism these prohibitions are not obligatory: many, after studying the tradition, decide for themselves not to eat pork and seafood.

questions.prompt: You are told that shechitah is cruelty and that it would be simpler to buy ordinary meat. What will you answer about shechitah and about the prohibition of blood?
questions.modelAnswer: The Torah says that blood is the soul: a person may eat meat, but not the life of the animal, so the blood of mammals and birds is forbidden. For me shechitah is not cruelty but a mitzvah: the shochet, with one swift cut of a smooth knife, lets the blood flow out, and tradition sees in this a prohibition against causing the animal unnecessary suffering. If the animal died on its own or was killed in another way, it is a nevelah, and I do not eat such meat even when the species is kosher. The Written Torah does not describe the method of slaughter, but the words “as I have commanded you” show that the laws of shechitah were transmitted orally.
keyPoints: Blood is the soul: one may eat meat, but not the life of the animal
Shechitah — a swift cut with a smooth knife, tied to the prohibition of unnecessary suffering
Another method of slaughter or a natural death — a nevelah
The laws of shechitah were transmitted orally: “as I have commanded you”
questions.explanation: The beit din listens to whether the candidate can calmly explain the meaning of blood and shechitah, not just recite a list of terms.

differs.text: Reform Judaism does not consider shechitah obligatory: the candidate may explain the tradition and choose kosher meat, vegetarianism, or meat with ethical labeling.

questions.prompt: May one cook meat with milk if you will not eat it yourself, but will feed it to an animal or sell it?
questions.modelAnswer: No, that is not permitted. The verse “do not cook a kid in its mother's milk” is repeated three times in the Torah, and the Sages derive three prohibitions: not to cook meat with milk, not to eat such a mixture, and not to benefit from it. Benefit includes, for example, selling the mixture or feeding it to one's own animal, so the words “I won't eat it myself” do not remove the prohibition. By Torah law this concerns the meat of domestic cattle; the Sages extended the prohibition to poultry, while fish does not fall under it. The Torah does not explain the reason — this is a chok; commentators see mercy in it, but I keep the prohibition because the Almighty so commanded.
keyPoints: Three prohibitions: cooking, eating, and benefiting
Benefit includes selling and feed for one's own animal
By Torah law — meat of domestic cattle; the Sages extended the prohibition to poultry
This is a chok: the interpretation about mercy does not replace the prohibition itself
questions.explanation: The beit din checks whether the candidate understands that the prohibition is broader than “not eating meat and milk from one plate.”

differs.text: In Reform Judaism the separation of meat and dairy is a personal choice: many simply do not mix them in one dish and do not treat the prohibition of benefit as an obligation.

questions.prompt: Cold cheese was placed on a clean meat plate, and non-kosher soup was once cooked in a metal pot. What will you do in each case?
questions.modelAnswer: If cold cheese was placed on a clean meat plate, taste is usually not transferred, and it is enough to wash the plate well. It is a different matter with a pot in which non-kosher soup was cooked: it absorbed the forbidden taste through the boiling liquid. Kashering follows the rule “as it absorbed, so it gives out”: metal that absorbed taste through liquid is immersed in boiling water — this is hagalah — while what was roasted over fire is heated until glowing. Before that the dishes are thoroughly cleaned and usually left unused for a day. If a case is doubtful — for example, a sharp onion was cut with a meat knife, or food lay in a dish for a long time — I do not decide on my own but ask a rabbi.
keyPoints: Cold contact usually transfers no taste: wash the plate
Hot liquid is absorbed: kasher by the same method
Hagalah — boiling water for pots; fire — for what was roasted over fire
Sharp foods, long soaking, and doubtful cases — a question for the rabbi
questions.explanation: The beit din checks whether the candidate distinguishes an ordinary cold contact from absorption of taste and does not kasher everything at random.

differs.text: In Reform practice, fully koshering the kitchen and two sets of dishes are usually not required. Tell what order of food and dishes you already keep, what of the classical laws you know, and what standard you consciously take upon yourself. If you are just now setting up a stricter kitchen — describe the steps in your own words.

questions.prompt: According to the Talmud, what atones for a person now that there is no Temple and no altar?
options: A person's table
Fasting on Monday and Thursday
A candle lit in the synagogue
A donation toward repairing the synagogue
questions.explanation: The Talmud says: as long as the Temple stood, the altar atoned; now “a person's table atones for him.” Kashrut, blessings, and words of Torah turn a meal into service.

questions.prompt: In halacha, what is the word “kosher” applied to?
options: Only to meat slaughtered by shechitah
To everything fit according to the law: food, a Torah scroll, a mezuzah, a shofar, and a mikveh
Only to products bearing a rabbi's seal
Only to dishes after kashering
questions.explanation: In halacha, everything fit for use according to the law is called “kosher”: not only food, but also a Torah scroll, a mezuzah, a shofar, and a mikveh.
questions.source: Lesson: What Is Kashrut and Why Is It Needed

questions.prompt: Why is salt traditionally placed on the bread at a meal?
options: So that the bread stays fresh longer
To tell a meat meal from a dairy one
This is required by the law of salting meat
In memory of the sacrifices in the Temple, which were salted
questions.explanation: The table is likened to the altar, and the sacrifices in the Temple were salted (Vayikra 2:13), so salt is placed on the bread.
questions.source: Lesson: What Is Kashrut and Why Is It Needed (Vayikra 2:13)

questions.prompt: Who objected to explaining kashrut by hygiene alone, saying that otherwise the Torah would be a medical book?
options: Rashi
Ramban
Abarbanel
Mar Ukva
questions.explanation: Rambam wrote in the Guide for the Perplexed (3:48) about the harm forbidden food does to the body, and Abarbanel and others objected: if it were only a matter of hygiene, the Torah would be a medical book.
questions.source: Lesson: What Is Kashrut and Why Is It Needed; Rambam, Guide for the Perplexed 3:48

questions.prompt: According to Pirkei Avot, three who ate at one table and spoke words of Torah are as though they ate from the table of the Almighty.
questions.explanation: Thus the lesson conveys the words of Pirkei Avot 3:3 (in some editions 3:4): words of Torah at a meal liken one's table to the table of the Almighty.

questions.prompt: Ramban explains the prohibition of birds of prey by the fact that their meat is harmful to health.
questions.explanation: Ramban speaks of the education of character: the predatory nature of such birds may pass to the one who eats them and breed cruelty. The argument about health is given by Rambam.

questions.prompt: The laws of shechitah and forbidden foods are discussed in detail in the Talmudic tractate “Berachot.”
questions.explanation: They are discussed in detail in the tractate Chullin; they were then codified by Rambam in the Mishneh Torah and in the Shulchan Aruch, in the section Yoreh Deah. Berachot 55a in this lesson is about a person's table, not a code of slaughtering laws.
questions.source: Lesson: What Is Kashrut and Why Is It Needed

questions.prompt: Match the group of mitzvot with its description.
pairs: Understood by reason: the prohibitions of theft and murder
They recall events of history: the holidays
Decrees without an explanation: the red heifer
questions.explanation: The Sages divide the mitzvot into mishpatim, edot, and chukim; kashrut largely belongs to the chukim.
questions.source: Lesson: What Is Kashrut and Why Is It Needed

questions.prompt: What is the name of the prohibition of mixing wool and linen — a classic chok alongside kashrut?
questions.explanation: In the lesson, shaatnez is named among the classic chukim together with the law of the red heifer and the laws of kashrut.
questions.source: Lesson: What Is Kashrut and Why Is It Needed

questions.prompt: A member of the beit din asks: “Why do people say that a person's table is like the altar? What does that look like in your home?”
questions.modelAnswer: I know the words of the Talmud: after the destruction of the Temple, a person's table atones in its place, as the altar once did. For me this means that dinner is not just food. I eat only kosher food, say blessings before and after eating, wash my hands before bread, and place salt on the bread, as the sacrifices were salted. I try to make words of Torah heard at the table — as Pirkei Avot says of three who spoke words of Torah at a meal.
keyPoints: Berachot 55a: the table atones, like the altar
Kashrut, blessings, washing of hands
Salt on the bread in memory of the sacrifices
Words of Torah at the table (Avot 3:3)
questions.explanation: The lesson shows how kashrut, together with blessings and words of Torah, turns a meal into service.

questions.prompt: A member of the beit din asks: “Is kashrut just a list of animals? What other topics do these laws include?”
questions.modelAnswer: No, the list of animals is only the beginning. Kashrut includes shechitah and the post-slaughter inspection, the prohibitions of blood, chelev, and the gid hanasheh, the prohibition of mixing meat with milk, and the laws of dishes. The laws about wine, bread, and food cooked by a non-Jew stand apart: these are mainly enactments of the Sages. The Written Torah gives the foundation, and the Oral Torah explains how to fulfill it — the tractate Chullin, Rambam, and Yoreh Deah.
keyPoints: Not only animals: shechitah, blood, chelev, gid hanasheh
Meat with milk and dishes
Wine, bread, and food of non-Jews — mainly from the Sages
Details — in Chullin and Yoreh Deah
questions.explanation: The lesson lists the makeup of the laws of kashrut: from the signs of animals to the enactments of the Sages about wine and food cooked by a non-Jew.
questions.source: Lesson: What Is Kashrut and Why Is It Needed

questions.prompt: Why is the camel not kosher?
options: It is a predator
It chews the cud, but its hooves are not cloven
It has cloven hooves, but it does not chew the cud
It lives in the desert, not in a herd
questions.explanation: The camel, like the hyrax and the hare, chews the cud but does not have cloven hooves, and both signs are required at once.

questions.prompt: Which caviar is kosher (with supervision of production)?
options: Black sturgeon caviar
Catfish caviar
Eel caviar
Red salmon caviar
questions.explanation: Salmon is a kosher fish, so its roe is kosher; the sturgeon is not kosher by the Orthodox position, and what comes from a non-kosher creature is non-kosher.
questions.source: Lesson: Permitted animals, birds, and fish

questions.prompt: How do the Torah's laws about birds differ from the laws about mammals and fish?
options: The Torah gives no signs but lists the forbidden species
The Torah permits all birds except birds of prey
For birds the Torah gives three signs instead of two
Birds do not require shechitah
questions.explanation: For animals and fish the Torah names signs, while for birds it only lists the forbidden species (Vayikra 11:13–19; Devarim 14:11–20).

questions.prompt: How many impure species of birds does the Talmud count?
questions.explanation: The Talmud (Chullin 63b) counts 24 non-kosher species; among them are the eagle, the hawk, the owl, the raven, the stork, and the ostrich.

questions.prompt: Which small creatures in food does the prohibition of insects apply to in halacha?
options: Any, even those visible only under a microscope
Only those larger than a centimeter
Only live ones at the moment of eating
Those visible to the naked eye
questions.explanation: What is visible to the naked eye is forbidden; microscopic organisms, discernible only under magnification, are not forbidden.
questions.source: Lesson: Permitted animals, birds, and fish

questions.prompt: An egg with a blood spot may be used if the spot is small.
questions.explanation: An egg with blood is not used. Therefore eggs are cracked one at a time into a transparent glass and each is checked (Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 66).

questions.prompt: The dye carmine (E120) is kosher because it is obtained from plants.
questions.explanation: Carmine is obtained from cochineal insects, so products containing it are not kosher; this is one of the reasons to buy ready-made products with a hechsher.
questions.source: Lesson: Permitted animals, birds, and fish

questions.prompt: Match the sign from Mishnah Chullin 3:6 with its meaning.
pairs: Not kosher according to the Mishnah
The extra toe of a kosher bird
Must be present in a kosher bird
questions.explanation: The Mishnah names the signs of a kosher bird, but in practice they are not sufficient: only birds with a mesorah are eaten. The question checks the signs themselves.

questions.prompt: Four species of which insect does the Torah permit as food?
questions.explanation: The exception to the prohibition of insects is four species of locusts (Vayikra 11:22); the tradition of identifying them has been preserved only in the Yemenite and some North African communities.

questions.prompt: The Torah names four species of locusts as permitted. Why do most communities still not eat locusts?
questions.modelAnswer: Vayikra 11:22 permits four species of locusts, and this is the only exception to the prohibition of insects. But these species can be identified only through an unbroken tradition. It has been preserved in the Yemenite and some North African communities. The others have no such tradition, so they do not eat locusts, while all other insects the Torah forbids outright.
keyPoints: The Torah's exception is four species of locusts (Vayikra 11:22)
The tradition was preserved in the Yemenite and some North African communities
Without the tradition, locusts are not eaten
questions.explanation: The Torah's permission applies where the tradition of identification has been preserved; most communities do not have it.

questions.prompt: A member of the beit din asks: “Besides meat, which products of animal origin do you check for kashrut, and why?”
questions.modelAnswer: I remember the rule: what comes out of a non-kosher creature is non-kosher. Therefore mare's or camel's milk, eggs of non-kosher birds, and roe of non-kosher fish are forbidden to me. I buy red salmon roe only with supervision, and I do not eat black sturgeon caviar. I eat honey without worry: the bee does not produce it with its body but only gathers it.
keyPoints: What comes out of a non-kosher creature is non-kosher (Mishnah Bechorot 1:2)
Milk, eggs, and roe of non-kosher species are forbidden
Honey is an exception (Bechorot 7b)
questions.explanation: The lesson explains the rule about products of non-kosher animals and the exception for honey.

questions.prompt: What is cut in shechitah?
options: Only the carotid artery
The spine at the base of the skull
The trachea and esophagus: most of both in cattle, most of one in poultry
The heart artery through the chest
questions.explanation: Shechitah is one unbroken cut across the throat. The halachic landmarks are the trachea and esophagus: in cattle most of both are cut, in poultry most of one is enough. The carotid arteries and jugular veins are severed together with them.
questions.source: Lesson: Shechitah, blood, chelev, and gid hanasheh

questions.prompt: What reason for the prohibition of blood does the verse of the Torah itself give?
options: Blood spoils the taste of meat
Blood is the soul
Blood belongs to the kohanim
Blood is dangerous to health
questions.explanation: “Only be firm not to eat the blood, for the blood is the soul”: a person is allowed to eat meat, but not the life of the animal.

questions.prompt: On which animals does the prohibition of the sciatic nerve (gid hanasheh) apply?
options: To domestic and wild animals, but not to birds
Only to the ox, the sheep, and the goat
To all animals and birds
Only to wild animals
questions.explanation: Unlike chelev, which is forbidden only in domestic cattle, the gid hanasheh is forbidden in both domestic and wild animals, but not in birds.

questions.prompt: What is shuman and what is its status?
options: Forbidden fat near the kidneys; it is removed during nikur
Fat of birds, forbidden by the Sages
Ordinary fat interspersed in the meat — it is permitted
Fat that was burned on the altar in the Temple
questions.explanation: Chelev is the special fat around the stomach, kidneys, and intestines that was offered on the altar; ordinary fat within the meat (shuman) is permitted.
questions.source: Lesson: Shechitah, blood, chelev, and gid hanasheh; Vayikra 7:23

questions.prompt: How can meat that was not salted and not rinsed within 72 hours after shechitah be kashered?
options: By double salting
By soaking for a day
It can no longer be kashered
Only by roasting over fire
questions.explanation: Meat not salted and not rinsed within 72 hours after shechitah can be kashered only by roasting over fire.
questions.source: Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 36; Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 69

questions.prompt: Fish and locusts do not require shechitah.
questions.explanation: The lesson states directly: shechitah is needed for kosher animals and birds, while fish and locusts do not require it.
questions.source: Lesson: Shechitah, blood, chelev, and gid hanasheh

questions.prompt: In the strict sense, the term “glatt” applies only to the lungs of large cattle.
questions.explanation: “Glatt” means that the animal's lungs are smooth, free of adhesions; the label “glatt kosher” on chicken or cheese is merely an advertising way of saying “strict kashrut.”

questions.prompt: Match the term with its meaning.
pairs: Removal of chelev and the sciatic nerve
Salting of meat to remove the blood
Covering the blood of birds and game with earth
The prohibition of causing animals unnecessary suffering
questions.explanation: Nikur is the removal of chelev and the sciatic nerve, melichah is salting against blood. Kisuy hadam is done after the shechitah of a bird or a wild animal, not of domestic cattle. Tzaar baalei chayim is the prohibition of causing animals unnecessary suffering.
questions.source: Lesson: Shechitah, blood, chelev, and gid hanasheh; Vayikra 17:13

questions.prompt: What is the name of the special Jewish method of slaughter, without which even a cow or a chicken is forbidden as food?
questions.explanation: Even an animal kosher in species is forbidden if it was not slaughtered by shechitah; otherwise it is a nevelah.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the punishment of “cutting off of the soul” that the Torah assigns for the intentional consumption of blood?
questions.explanation: For the intentional violation of the prohibition of blood the Torah assigns karet (Vayikra 7:27).

questions.prompt: Explain why an animal can turn out to be treif even after a proper shechitah, and what “glatt” means for Sephardim and Ashkenazim.
questions.modelAnswer: After shechitah the internal organs are inspected. If a defect is found because of which the animal would not have lived out the year — for example, a perforated organ — it is treif even if the shechitah was proper; the main defects are listed in Mishnah Chullin 3:1. In cattle the lungs must be checked for adhesions — sirchot. “Glatt” means the lungs are completely smooth: Sephardim by the Beit Yosef eat only such meat, while Ashkenazim by the Rema allow some easily removable adhesions, though many today also buy “glatt.” I will buy meat with a reliable hechsher and follow the custom I determine with my rabbi.
keyPoints: A defect with which it would not have lived out the year — treif
Checking the lungs for sirchot
Sephardim — only glatt (Beit Yosef)
Ashkenazim by the Rema are more lenient
questions.explanation: The lesson distinguishes the correctness of shechitah from the inspection of organs and explains the different customs about “glatt.”
questions.source: Mishnah Chullin 3:1; Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 39

questions.prompt: According to the Shulchan Aruch, what is it sufficient to do after dairy food before eating meat?
options: Rinse the mouth, eat something pareve, wash the hands, and change the tablecloth and dishes
Wait six hours
Wait until the next day
Nothing: meat may be eaten right after dairy
questions.explanation: According to the Shulchan Aruch (Yoreh Deah 89:2), after dairy one rinses the mouth, eats something neutral, washes the hands, and changes the tablecloth and dishes. Many Ashkenazim by custom wait another half an hour or an hour. The exception is hard aged cheese.

differs.text: In Reform Judaism, many families that separate meat and dairy do not observe these rules of transition and waiting times.

questions.prompt: May two people who know each other eat meat and cheese at the same table if there is no divider between them?
options: Yes, if each has his own plate
No: a noticeable divider is needed — a separate tablecloth or an object between them
No: they may not even be in the same room
Yes: the prohibition concerns only cooking in one pot
questions.explanation: If two people who know each other eat together, one eating meat and the other cheese, a noticeable dividing sign (*eiker*) is needed: a separate tablecloth, a placemat, or an object between the plates (Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 88).

questions.prompt: How does the Rambam explain why one must wait after meat before eating dairy?
options: The fat of meat leaves an aftertaste in the mouth for a long time
Meat takes a long time to digest in the stomach
Shreds of meat get stuck between the teeth
That is how offerings were separated in the Temple
questions.explanation: According to the Rambam, shreds of meat get stuck between the teeth; the explanation about the aftertaste of fat is the opinion of Rashi.
questions.source: Lesson: Meat and Dairy (Rambam; Rashi; Chullin 105a)

questions.prompt: After which dairy product, by the custom of the strict cited by the Rema, does one wait as long as after meat?
options: After sour cream
After butter
After fresh cottage cheese
After hard cheese aged six months or more
questions.explanation: The Rema (Yoreh Deah 89:2) cites the custom of waiting after hard aged cheese as after meat; hard usually means cheese aged six months or more.

questions.prompt: Halacha requires marking meat dishes red and dairy dishes blue.
questions.explanation: Color coding is a convenient custom, not a law.

questions.prompt: Fish may not be eaten together with meat under the same prohibition as meat with dairy.
questions.explanation: Fish does not fall under the meat-and-dairy prohibition. It is not eaten or cooked together with meat for another reason: the Talmud speaks of a health hazard (Pesachim 76b; Yoreh Deah 116:2). Between fish and meat one rinses the mouth or eats a piece of bread.

questions.prompt: The waiting hours after meat are counted from the beginning of the meat meal.
questions.explanation: The count runs from the end of the meat meal to the beginning of the dairy meal.

questions.prompt: Match the word with its meaning.
questions.explanation: Basari and chalavi are the Hebrew names for meat and dairy; fleishik and milchik are their names in Yiddish.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the Talmudic sage whose account of his father and of himself became the source of the custom of waiting after meat?
questions.explanation: Mar Ukva related that his father, after eating meat, would not eat cheese until the next day, while he himself waited until the next meal (Chullin 105a).

questions.prompt: A beit din member asks: “How long will you wait after meat, and how did you choose this custom?”
questions.modelAnswer: I know that there are different customs: most communities wait six hours, many Jews of German origin wait three hours, and Dutch Jews wait one hour. A person usually follows the custom of his family, and I have no such family tradition. Therefore I discussed this with a rabbi and adopted the custom of the community I am joining. I count from the end of the meat meal, and after dairy I rinse my mouth, eat a piece of bread, and wash my hands.
keyPoints: Customs of 6, 3, and 1 hour
A ger chooses together with a rabbi
Usually — the custom of one's own community
questions.explanation: The lesson says that one who has undergone giyur chooses the waiting custom together with a rabbi, most often according to the custom of his community.

differs.text: In Reform Judaism many do not keep the waiting hours, but only avoid mixing meat and milk in one dish; this is a personal choice.

questions.prompt: What is the main principle of koshering dishes?
options: Any dishes need only be washed with soap
Dishes are kashered only by fire
As it absorbed, so it expels
New dishes are always kosher
questions.explanation: Dishes are cleaned by the same method through which the taste entered them: what absorbed taste through boiling water is kashered with boiling water, and what absorbed it through fire — by fire.

questions.prompt: From which account in the Torah are the laws of kashering dishes derived?
options: About the spoils after the war with Midian
About the Exodus from Egypt
About the building of the Mishkan (Tabernacle)
About the Flood and Noah's ark
questions.explanation: Moshe and Elazar the kohen ordered the metal vessels of Midian to be passed through fire or through water.

questions.prompt: Why is glassware bought from a non-Jew immersed in a mikveh?
options: Glass absorbs more taste than metal
By enactment of the sages: glass, like metal, can be re-melted
The Torah says so directly about the vessels of Midian
To remove traces of non-kosher food
questions.explanation: Metal dishes are immersed by a mitzvah of the Torah, and glass ones by enactment of the sages, because glass, like metal, can be re-melted.
questions.source: Avodah Zarah 75b; Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 120

questions.prompt: What reason does the lesson give for the prohibition of cheese made without Jewish supervision (gevinat akum)?
options: The concern that milk of non-kosher animals might be mixed in
Cheese may not be eaten raw
Cheese is made on Shabbat
Rennet from the stomachs of animals not slaughtered according to kashrut
questions.explanation: Gevinat akum is forbidden, in particular because of rennet from the stomachs of animals not slaughtered according to kashrut; the concern about the admixture of non-kosher milk is the reason for the prohibition of chalav akum.
questions.source: Lesson: Vessels and the Kitchen; Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 115

differs.text: Masorti is more lenient than Orthodoxy on the question of cheeses; the specific rules should be clarified with the community rabbi.

questions.prompt: Before kashering, dishes are usually cleaned thoroughly and not used for 24 hours.
questions.explanation: Dishes are cleaned of rust, burnt-on residue, and food remains, and usually left unused for a day so that they cease to be “ben yomo.”

questions.prompt: R. Moshe Feinstein prohibited any milk for which no Jew was present at the milking, even under strict government supervision.
questions.explanation: Some authorities, in particular R. Moshe Feinstein, permitted milk under strict government supervision, although many observe chalav Yisrael.
questions.source: Lesson: Vessels and the Kitchen; Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 115

questions.prompt: Match the enactment of the sages with what it concerns.
pairs: A dish cooked by a non-Jew
Bread baked by a non-Jew at home
Milk for whose milking no Jew was present
questions.explanation: The lesson lists these enactments about food that consists of kosher products but is prepared by a non-Jew.

questions.prompt: What is the immersion in a mikveh of dishes made by or bought from a non-Jew called?
questions.explanation: This is the mitzvah of tevilat keilim: it is derived from the passage about the vessels of Midian, and it brings the item into the holiness of a Jewish home.

questions.prompt: You bought new metal pots and glass cups at an ordinary store. What will you do before first use?
questions.modelAnswer: New dishes have absorbed no non-kosher taste, but metal and glass dishes from a non-Jew must be immersed in a mikveh — this is tevilat keilim. First I will wash them and remove all stickers and glue, so that nothing separates the water from the surface. Before the immersion I will say the blessing “al tevilat keilim,” because there are several items. Each item I will immerse completely in one motion, holding it loosely, so that the water touches every surface.
keyPoints: Metal and glass from a non-Jew are immersed even when new
Remove the stickers and glue
The blessing “al tevilat keilim”
Complete immersion in one motion
questions.explanation: The lesson describes the order of tevilat keilim and stresses that even new dishes require immersion.
questions.source: Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 120:3; Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 37

questions.prompt: Why did the sages prohibit food cooked by a non-Jew (bishul akum) if all the products in it are kosher? What will you do?
questions.modelAnswer: The sages enacted these prohibitions in order to preserve the separateness of the Jewish community, to prevent intermarriage, and to guard against mistakes in kashrut. Bishul akum concerns dishes that are not eaten raw and that are fit for “a king's table” — for example, meat, fish, eggs, potatoes. For food to be “bishul Yisrael,” a Jew must take part in the cooking: by Ashkenazi custom it is enough to light the fire, by Sephardi custom — to place the food on the fire or to stir it. Therefore I eat in restaurants where the fire is lit by the mashgiach, and at home I cook myself and clarify my custom with a rabbi.
keyPoints: Purpose: the community's separateness, protection from intermarriage and mistakes
Dishes that are not eaten raw and are fit for “a king's table”
Ashkenazim: a Jew lights the fire; Sephardim: he places it on the fire
Clarify the custom with a rabbi
questions.explanation: The lesson explains the purpose of the sages' enactments and the difference between the Ashkenazi and Sephardi customs regarding bishul akum.
questions.source: Avodah Zarah 35b–38a; Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 113

differs.text: Masorti is more lenient than Orthodoxy on questions of food cooked by a non-Jew; the position should be clarified with the community rabbi.

questions.prompt: How does the blessing over wine end?
options: …borei pri ha-etz
…borei pri ha-adamah
…borei minei mezonot
…borei pri ha-gafen
questions.explanation: Over wine one says “borei pri ha-gafen” — “Who creates the fruit of the vine.”

questions.prompt: Why might an ordinary-looking cookie without a hechsher turn out to be non-kosher?
options: It may have been baked on a weekday
It may contain gelatin, whey, carmine, or wine
Any baked goods require shechitah
Cookies are always considered meat
questions.explanation: Ready-made products can contain hidden ingredients — gelatin, carmine, whey, wine — and they may be produced on the same line as non-kosher food.
questions.source: Lesson: Hechsher, Wine, and Kashrut Across the Movements

questions.prompt: What does the marking “DE” next to a kashrut symbol mean?
options: The product was made on dairy equipment
The product is kosher for Pesach
The product is meat
The product is certified in Germany
questions.explanation: D means dairy, and DE means the product was made on dairy equipment; this matters for those who eat it after meat.
questions.source: Lesson: Hechsher, Wine, and Kashrut Across the Movements

questions.prompt: What is the “Magen Tzedek”?
options: The Israeli kashrut level “mehadrin”
A Reform book on food ethics
The ethical symbol of the Masorti movement as a supplement to the hechsher
Supervision of the Eda HaChareidit rabbinical court
questions.explanation: In the 2000s the initiative “Magen Tzedek” appeared in the Masorti movement — an ethical symbol as a supplement to the hechsher.
questions.source: Lesson: Hechsher, Wine, and Kashrut Across the Movements

questions.prompt: A kosher restaurant must display a valid kashrut certificate with the date and the name of the organization.
questions.explanation: The lesson says that a kosher restaurant displays a valid teudat kashrut with the date and the name of the organization.
questions.source: Lesson: Hechsher, Wine, and Kashrut Across the Movements

questions.prompt: In Israel a plant product needs only a hechsher on the ingredients: terumot, maasrot, orlah, and shemitah are not checked separately.
questions.explanation: The lesson says that in Israel products of plant origin are also checked for the agricultural mitzvot: terumah and maaser, orlah, and shemitah. An ordinary list of ingredients is not enough for this.
questions.source: Lesson: Hechsher, Wine, and Kashrut Across the Movements

questions.prompt: Match the kashrut designation with its meaning.
pairs: Supervision by a rabbinical court (beit din tzedek)
A higher level of stringency in Israel
questions.explanation: The lesson explains these designations; it is important to look at which organization stands behind the symbol.
questions.source: Lesson: Hechsher, Wine, and Kashrut Across the Movements

questions.prompt: What is the specialist who supervises kashrut at a production site, in a restaurant, or in a kitchen called?
questions.explanation: Mashgiach — “one who supervises,” a kashrut specialist.
questions.source: Lesson: Hechsher, Wine, and Kashrut Across the Movements

questions.prompt: A beit din member asks: “How do you choose products in an ordinary supermarket?”
questions.modelAnswer: I buy ready-made products only with a hechsher, because they can contain gelatin, carmine, whey, or wine, and production may run on the same line as non-kosher food. A single letter “K” is not enough for me: I look at which organization stands behind the symbol and rely on those approved by my rabbi. I check the markings: D means dairy, and P means kosher for Pesach, not “pareve.” I also use lists of checked products published by rabbinates.
keyPoints: Ready-made products need a hechsher
A single letter “K” is no guarantee
Read the markings D, DE, P
Hechshers recognized by one's own rabbi
questions.explanation: The lesson explains why a hechsher is needed and how to read the markings.
questions.source: Lesson: Hechsher, Wine, and Kashrut Across the Movements

questions.prompt: How do the approaches of Orthodox, Conservative, and Reform Judaism to kashrut differ?
questions.modelAnswer: For Orthodox Judaism kashrut is obligatory halacha in its full scope, both the laws of the Torah and the enactments of the sages; the candidate keeps a fully kosher home with a recognized hechsher. The Conservative movement also considers kashrut obligatory halacha and expects a kosher home, but its Committee on Jewish Law and Standards (CJLS) is more lenient on particular questions, for example about wine from non-Jews and some cheeses. Reform Judaism, in the Pittsburgh Platform of 1885, declared the laws of food non-obligatory, and today sees in kashrut a conscious personal choice and “ethical kashrut.” I understand which approach is accepted in my community and am ready to live by it.
keyPoints: Orthodoxy: everything is obligatory, including the enactments of the sages
Masorti: halacha, but CJLS decisions are more lenient in particulars
Reform: from Pittsburgh 1885 to a conscious choice
Ethical kashrut
questions.explanation: The lesson describes the attitude to kashrut in the three movements and its history among Reform Jews.
questions.source: Pittsburgh Platform (1885); “Statement of Principles of Reform Judaism” (1999)

differs.text: A Reform rabbi does not require a kosher kitchen, but expects knowledge of the laws and a thoughtful personal decision.
Masorti expects a kosher home, but on wine, cheeses, and food cooked by a non-Jew the decisions of the CJLS are more lenient than the Orthodox ones.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the kitchen of a Reform home?
options: Two sets of dishes are not required; what matters is knowledge of the laws, an honest measure of practice, and often the ethical side of food
The kitchen must be fully kosher according to the Shulchan Aruch, otherwise the giyur is invalid
Reform Jews are forbidden to have any dishes at home at all
Kashrut is not a topic of conversation in a Reform home
questions.explanation: The Reform path asks for knowledge and an honest measure, not obligatory double sinks. “I observe nothing because it is permitted” is a weak answer.
questions.source: Lesson “Vessels and the Kitchen,” section on the Reform home

questions.prompt: It is enough for a Reform candidate to say “kashrut is not obligatory for us,” without studying the laws of permitted animals, blood, and mixing meat with milk.
questions.explanation: A conscious choice begins with knowledge of the classical categories. Ignorance does not replace a principle.
questions.source: Lesson on the kitchen; lesson on kashrut across the movements

questions.prompt: The food laws of the Torah remain in force: they cannot be declared annulled by a new teaching.
questions.explanation: Kashrut consists of the mitzvot of the Torah. No prophet has the right to annul them (Devarim 13:1; Rambam, Foundations of the Torah 9:1).
questions.source: Devarim 13:1; Vayikra 11; Rambam, Foundations of the Torah 9:1

questions.prompt: Why is kashrut not considered “no longer needed” once a person has “believed in” a new teaching?
options: Because the Torah is eternal, and its mitzvot are not annulled
Because kashrut was invented only in the Middle Ages
Because kashrut is needed only in the Land of Israel
Because it is purely medical advice
questions.explanation: The Rambam's ninth principle and Devarim 13:1: the Torah is not replaced and not diminished.
